articles.title_orig: The US and China Cannot Slow the AI Race, But They Can Make It Safer - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The US and China Cannot Slow the AI Race, But They Can Make It Safer - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
The most important shift in artificial intelligence (AI) is not that models are becoming more intelligent, but that they are becoming more capable of acting.
Much of the first wave of AI safety governance focused on misinformation, bias, deepfakes, privacy violations and harmful content. Those risks remain. But increasingly capable AI agents can plan, write and execute code, use tools, obtain credentials, and interact with external systems. Recent incidents in which OpenAI’s autonomous systems slipped past their constraints show that as agents gain tools and autonomy, the boundary between a model and the outside world becomes harder to enforce.
That makes AI safety a collective-action problem. The AI superpowers face a prisoner’s dilemma. If one laboratory slows while competitors continue, it may lose its edge. Disclosure creates a similar tension: reporting failures can make the wider ecosystem safer, but the discloser bears the costs and may expose vulnerabilities to attackers. Governments face the same strategic impasse as the firms. Washington fears that slowing its AI development will allow China to catch up; Beijing fears that doing so will leave it further behind.
Yet cooperation can be narrow on AI safety. The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in such cooperation. It has an interest in ensuring that AI-enabled cyber incidents are contained before they cascade through third countries, shared software infrastructure and global supply chains. China has the same systemic interest.
This collective action has significant implications for middle-power countries. Helping others repair a vulnerability can be a form of systemic containment and a public good.
The AI arms race is intensifying.
U.S. President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow U.S. AI development, framing continued technological leadership as essential to winning the AI race . On September 29, he convened major technology companies at the White House, where six firms – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia – signed a voluntary accord built around four layers of oversight: internal capability assessments, internal audit teams, independent external auditors, and board-level review. His administration ordered federal agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “ super intelligence ,” presenting the technology as a source of economic and strategic leadership.
Taken together, these moves point to a U.S. approach combining continued AI power with developer responsibility, voluntary industry controls, external scrutiny, and ex-post legal accountability.
China approaches the problem through a more centrally coordinated system. In May 2026, guidelines on AI agents , issued jointly by the Cyberspace Administration of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, made “safety and controllability” a baseline requirement for agent development and deployment. Governance is tiered, with tighter filing, testing and recall requirements for agents used in sensitive sectors.
On September 14, China’s AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 reiterated “safety and controllability” while updating its classification of AI risks and associated technical and governance measures.
Despite their institutional differences, the two approaches converge on one point: neither country wants safety policy to halt AI development, and both increasingly recognize that greater autonomy creates new problems of control.
Common Ground and Shared Risks
AI systems rest on overlapping technological foundations. Chinese AI development has relied heavily on U.S. chips and, in some cases, U.S. cloud infrastructure. Export controls may weaken those hardware links, but the stronger case for joint risk management lies in the software and services AI systems share.
Standards, certificates, identity infrastructure, model repositories, and open-source libraries support trust across networks. A compromised root certificate or a maintainer’s credentials can put the entire dependency tree at risk .
AI risks vary along two dimensions: severity of harm and whether responsible actors can recognize it in time. The biggest danger is severe and invisible harm, where nothing visibly breaks for days or weeks, yet time compounds the severity of the incident. An AI agent could quietly corrupt records, act on instructions planted in its memory or in documents it consults, or appear cooperative while accumulating access beyond operator intent. Infrastructure may operate normally while the means to disrupt it are already in place.
The dependencies and shared risks determine which code a system runs, which credentials it accepts, and which updates it trusts. Harm can cross borders quietly even when models and their owners remain separate.
That makes the speed of response critical. Delays in detecting a breach, assigning responsibility or authorizing a shutdown can allow damage to spread. Both China and the United States therefore need warnings to reach personnel with the authority and technical means to respond.
There is no obvious diplomatic agreement that can resolve the paradox built into the AI race: it rewards speed and secrecy, while safety depends on collective restraint and disclosure.
China-U.S. cooperation should instead focus on measures that improve safety without requiring either side to slow unilaterally, transfer its most advanced models, or expose commercially and strategically sensitive capabilities. Four areas stand out:
Before the Trump-Xi summit, American and Chinese security experts in a long-running bilateral dialogue proposed red lines around nuclear systems, human control over consequential cyber operations, and a dedicated mechanism for AI incidents.
When an AI agent can search, authenticate, write code, call external tools, and act within minutes or seconds, where should human intervention occur? Requiring approval for every step would undermine the autonomous value of AI agents; waiting until something goes wrong may make intervention too late.
The harder questions concern permissions, escalation thresholds, shutdown mechanisms and which actions should always require explicit human authorization. Researchers could cooperate on these engineering challenges without sharing model weights, training data, or proprietary frontier capabilities.
Sandboxing, monitoring, permission controls, and model-level refusals are often treated as established safeguards.
The underlying technical risk is broad: with appropriate tools and access, advanced models could identify previously unknown vulnerabilities and develop exploits across well-protected systems without step-by-step human direction. The key question is not whether a developer has guardrails, but whether they still work as agents become capable enough to search for ways around them.
While frontier AI labs in the U.S. have voluntarily disclosed instances of their models escaping from sandboxed environments, public reporting from China on comparable containment failures remains limited. This lack of transparency shouldn’t stop the two sides from working together. Washington and Beijing could develop compatible methods for testing sandbox escape, scope violations, unauthorized tool use, shutdown resistance, and failures of human intervention. Independent auditors, potentially from trusted third countries, could help verify the results.
Cyber attribution has always been challenging. AI makes it harder.
A defender discovering unauthorized access may be looking at a state-directed operation, a criminal actor using AI, a human-directed autonomous agent, or an agent that has exceeded its instructions while pursuing a legitimate task.

articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias strengthens to category three as evacuations orders issued along US Gulf Coast
articles.content_orig:

Isaias strengthened into a Category 3 hurricane on Friday as it surged toward the Gulf Coast, where final preparations were being made for potentially life-threatening storm surges and high winds.
The National Hurricane Center said the hurricane is set to make landfall late on Friday somewhere along the Alabama - Florida line.
Meanwhile, the weather event is expected to create dangerous conditions in the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi .
The Category 3 storm was packing 120 mph (193 kph) winds early on Friday before it was set to continue strengthening.
Category 3 storms can cause devastating damage, the center warned.
Isaias was expected to weaken quickly as it hits shore and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon as it moves north and inland along the Alabama-Mississippi line, the center said.
“Preparations should be rushed to completion as the weather will go downhill quickly today,” the hurricane center said in an early morning forecast. “While the storm is not expected to make landfall at peak intensity, it is likely that Isaias will still be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast.”
Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, was centered about 200 miles (322 kilometers) south-southeast of the mouth of the Mississippi River and moving to the north at about 15 mph (24 kph), the center said.
It was expected to make landfall between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and Choctawhatchee Bay in the Florida Panhandle in the evening.
Besides wind and storm surges, the hurricane will likely bring flash flooding and spawn tornadoes, the hurricane center said.
A hurricane warning was in place from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the western Florida Panhandle. Tropical storm warnings were issued from southeastern Louisiana to Aucilla River along Florida's Big Bend.
Preparations have been going on for days. On Thursday, residents boarded up windows and stacked sandbags while thousands of National Guard soldiers were deployed.
Isaias is expected to bring a storm surge as high as 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2 meters), with the deepest water hitting immediate coastal areas, along with large and dangerous waves, the hurricane center said.
Coastal communities moved quickly to prepare on Thursday, as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double-red beach flags signaled water access was closed.
Several counties announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties, with Florida’s Ron DeSantis saying about 5,000 National Guard troops were expected to mobilize by Friday.
On Dauphin Island, a 15-mile (24-kilometer) barrier island off the Alabama coast, officials encouraged voluntary evacuations, particularly on its popular western section, which is vulnerable to storm surge.
Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not anticipate substantial damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst.”
Meanwhile in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Simon, which formed as a tropical storm on Wednesday off of Mexico and became a hurricane late Thursday, was forecast to strengthen into a Category 4 hurricane.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran's Houthi allies kill 3 in strike on Saudi airport as Trump rules out pre-midterms strikes
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran's Houthi allies kill 3 in strike on Saudi airport as Trump rules out pre-midterms strikes
articles.content_orig:
President Trump teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks Friday at a Columbus Day celebration, but offered little information to speculate on what the announcement would be about.
Mr. Trump pointed out Energy Secretary Chris Wright and said he was "doing a great job."
"We have, I think, some big news on that diesel situation," the president said. "It's gonna — we're gonna be knocking the hell out of it. And remember, what have we done? We stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That's big time. And the prices — the prices will come tumbling."
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA , which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.
Diesel had never previously crossed $6 a gallon until just before Labor Day weekend. The record, hit on Sept. 22, was $6.53 per gallon. Diesel is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, so it's a factor for nearly every type of good, including groceries.
The Trump administration has looked into several ways to lower diesel prices, most recently signing an executive order this week allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways. Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.
Sri Lanka's government says it has no immediate plans to help 19 Iranian ships that have been anchored in the international waters near the island nation facing food, water and fuel shortages.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo said Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States.
He said, however, there hasn't been any communication from the U.S. warning of repercussions should Sri Lanka decide to help.
Rodrigo said the ships are stationed 24 nautical miles from Sri Lanka's coast and have reported shortages of food, water and fuel.
Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath told local Sunday Times newspaper the ships are Iranian oil tankers and they have been anchored off Sri Lanka for the past several months after the U.S. resumed its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving dozens of Iranian vessels stranded and unable to return home.
The U.K., France, Germany, Australia and Canada have advised their citizens against travel to parts of Saudi Arabia following a wave of Houthi attacks, including one that killed three civilians at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.
The U.K. Foreign Office now advises against all but essential travel to the Riyadh region, Najran, Jizan and Aseer provinces, Taif city and Taif International Airport, and against all travel within six miles of the Yemeni border.
France says travel to Najran, Abha, Khamis Muhsait and Djizan in the south of the kingdom " remains strongly discouraged ," and Germany , Australia and Canada have all advised against all travel to the country.
The U.S. has also tightened restrictions , requiring government employees to obtain special authorization to use Riyadh airport, and barring them from all travel within 20 miles of the Yemen border. U.S. government employees also require "special authorization for travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu, and Taif."
There is currently no warning for U.S. nationals more broadly to avoid Saudi Arabia, but the U.S. embassy in Riyadh urged Americans across the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance due to the complex security environment."
Yemeni government forces, backed by air support from the Saudi-led coalition, have taken control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Mayyun Island from the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, a Saudi diplomat said Friday.
Saudi Arabian Ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed Al Jaber, said in a post on X that the strait had been "cleansed" of remaining Houthi forces.
Fighting escalated dramatically this week after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive to retake territory held by Houthis, including some coastline around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that was seized by the rebels only weeks ago. The Houthis have held a vast portion of Yemen, including its capital Sanaa, for over a decade.
Yemeni forces claimed earlier this week to have retaken other key territory along the Red Sea coast, north of the strait, but the Houthis insisted Tuesday that their fighters still had " full control over all their gains on the ground. "
The Iran-backed Houthis appeared to taunt Saudi Arabia on Friday, as the group's spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree declared that humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh's airport would be allowed only with authorization from the Yemeni rebel group.
"Humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh airport will be allowed for all flights that have obtained a permit from the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center in the capital, Sanaa," Saree said in a post on X .
The statement was a challenge to Saudi Arabia's control of its own airspace. It came just a day after a Houthi attack killed three people at Riyadh's King Khaled International Airport, including a Saudia Airlines captain.
The Houthis warned international airlines on Monday that "operating in the skies of Saudi Arabia" would be "unsafe as long as the Saudi aggression against our country continues."
The statement from the Houthis' Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center (NOCC) said "the skies of Saudi Arabia will be a theater for operations by our armed forces," declaring that the rebel group would accept "no responsibility after this announcement" for anything that happens to aircraft.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday that its navy had struck a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tanker after it allegedly attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz via what it considers an illegal route through the waterway.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy said the vessel, identified as NV Sunshine, was struck "a few hours ago" as it "intended to cross via the illegal route," referring to a U.S.-backed lane that skirts close to the Omani coast.
On Wednesday, a senior IRGC advisor said Iran would soon block what it considers "illegal routes" through the Strait of Hormuz.
Brig. Gen. Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to the IRGC commander-in-chief, reiterated Iran's stance that the strait is closed and that Iranian armed forces have "full control" over it, adding that the situation would continue until Iran's "legitimate demands" are met.
The Trump administration insists the strait is open and that the southern route is safe for commercial vessels. The U.S. military has escorted some ships through that route for weeks, helping energy shipments from the Persian Gulf, which have been severely impeded by the ongoing war with Iran, rebound.
Germany is going to release up to 15 million barrels of diesel, crude and heating oil, the country's economy minister said Friday.
"Diesel ⁠and heating oil will be the first, with crude oil to follow," Katherina Reiche told the Reuters news agency, adding that Germany would implement an agreement reached by the G7 last week to release 100 million barrels of diesel oil .
"We must always have the entire supply chain ‌in mind. Available crude oil alone is not enough," she said.
The Trump administration has pressured Europe to draw on its emergency reserves.
Mr. Trump had threatened to ban U.S. diesel exports, a move that would push global diesel prices even higher, saying in late September that he had "called for" such a ban. But after the G7 announcement last week the president said "we were never going to do" it.
The president of the European Union's governing commission, Ursula von der Leyen, condemned on Friday the deadly Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia's main international airport the previous day, calling on Iran's proxy groups to "stop their reckless and violent acts."

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
articles.content_orig:
The ⁠ICC’s deputy prosecutor condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal’s work
Navi Pillay has begun giving a press conference after the declaration that she has won this year’s Nobel Peace prize. She began by saying she dedicates the award to “survivors of international crimes”.
She called on people to stand together in the defence of rule of law.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today .
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza ( 11:02 , 11:04 , 11:06 , 11:11 ).
In her first reaction, Pillay specifically paid tribute to all people defending human rights everywhere, as she joked to her associates that “if you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump” ( 11:53 , 12:02 ).
Her win was widely celebrated by senior judges and human right campaigners, who offered their congratulations ( 11:33 , 12:06 , 12:17 , 12:21 , 13:22 , 15:25 ), including the president of the international court of justice, of which she is a former judge ( 12:58 ).
But Israel reacted angrily to the award, saying that “it’s the grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice” ( 13:52 ).
US president Donald Trump also reposted a critical comment saying the Nobel committee “shamed itself beyond repair and demeaned” the prize ( 16:06 ).
Just hours after the announcement, which was explicitly meant as the Nobel Committee’s backing for the international court of justice, the US has imposed sanctions on the court ( 16:20 ).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
When the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not.
Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect.
A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government.
A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel. Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%.
Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion. Five countries chose to boycott the Eurovision song contest this year over Israel’s participation, after organisers declined to exclude it over its conduct in the Gaza war and rising violence in the West Bank. Organisers have now decided that broadcasters will no longer be eligible to host the song contest if their state is involved in an armed conflict or sensitive geopolitical situation.
More than 74,000 people, including at least 21,200 children, have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its war in retaliation for the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, in which the terrorist group killed 1,209 people – including 36 children – and took 251 hostages, inflicting a nationwide trauma .
Gaza remains a humanitarian catastrophe , with people facing acute shortages of water, nutritious food and medical equipment and medicines, while contending with disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the threat of death or injury. Israel’s airstrikes continue: the death toll includes 1,400 Palestinians killed since a ceasefire was declared a year ago.
The EU talks on the Middle East will focus on the conflicts in Iran and Yemen, but ministers will also discuss the situation in Gaza and the West Bank in the context of elections in Israel on 27 October and the first legislative elections in Palestine in 20 years, which are expected by late November.
The discussion is expected to expose familiar fault lines in the 27-member EU. One group of countries are vocal supporters of the Palestinian cause: Spain and Ireland were the first to call for a review of whether Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war was in breach of the human rights requirements of its association agreement with the EU, which covers the €68bn (£58bn) trade relationship, cooperation in research, environment and energy.
A second group consistently opposes targeting Israel’s government: Germany and Austria are close allies for historical reasons, while Czechia and Italy are ideologically aligned with Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration.
Among a third, larger group of countries in the middle are several, such as France and the Netherlands, that are increasingly critical of the Netanyahu government’s conduct in Gaza and its plans to build the vast E1 settlement, which threatens to critically damage the two-state solution.
Czechs go to the polls on Friday at the start of two days of voting to fill one-third of the seats in Parliament’s upper house, the Senate, and elect local representatives, AP reported.
The elections are the first test for populist billionaire Andrej Babiš since he returned to power after a decisive victory in parliamentary elections in October 2025.
His centrist ANO (YES) movement hopes to make gains in the 81-seat Senate, which is controlled by pro-western opposition parties. Twenty-seven Senate seats are up for grabs in the two-round election, with runoffs scheduled for next week. First-round results are expected on Saturday.
Babiš has formed a governing coalition with two small political groups whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine and rejecting some key European Union policies.
Unlike the government, the opposition and president Petr Pavel remain firm supporters of Ukraine following Russia’s invasion.
But Pavel – an avid biker – attracted a lot of attention in the build up to the vote as it emerged that he would miss the vote due to a long-planned motorcycle trip in Morocco. After days of relentless pressure, he eventually cut the holiday short and reported to vote, acknowledging his original “error” in scheduling.
“Some mistakes can be corrected relatively easily, others with more difficulty, and some cannot be corrected at all.
Fortunately, a mistake in planning can be remedied by changing the plan. Admitting a mistake is not easy, but if a politician values people’s trust, he must prove it.
I know what responsibility is and that any trust is hard to earn, but terribly easy and quick to lose. You pay for mistakes, and I have learned from this one of my own.”
The European Union is granting temporary trade preferences to Armenia following trade restrictions recently imposed by Russia.
In a move which shows how flexible the EU can be, it said the temporary trade preferences “will help alleviate the difficult situation faced by Armenian producers and exporters and support the resilience of Armenia’s economy by facilitating access to the EU market.
The measures, which will enter into force tomorrow for a period of two years, temporarily allow 80% of Armenian exports to the EU, including almost all exports of fresh fruit, vegetables and flowers affected by the Russian measures, as well as over 91% of exports of beverages and spirits.
Armenia is not an accession state, but has been singled out for support as part of the EU a broader solidarity support package

articles.title_orig: Scientists Took a Cheek Swab From the World's Oldest Tortoise. His DNA Could Reveal Hints to Longevity
articles.title_zh: Scientists Took a Cheek Swab From the World's Oldest Tortoise. His DNA Could Reveal Hints to Longevity
articles.content_orig:
Throughout world wars, pandemics and the turn of centuries, there was Jonathan. As the world around him shifted and changed, he lived the slow life munching grass on Saint Helena, a British island territory some 1,200 miles off the western coast of Africa.
The Aldabra giant tortoise is the oldest turtle in recorded history and the world’s oldest living land animal. Caretakers don’t know his exact age, but a photograph from 1882 shows the tortoise looking fully grown, which, for his species, is at least 50 years old. This means that Jonathan would be about 194 today.
“To be honest, I suspect he’s older,” veterinarian Joe Hollins, who looks after Jonathan, told the Washington Post ’s Cathy Free in 2022. “But we can never know.”
No matter Jonathan’s exact age, one thing seems certain: Something has made him exceptional when it comes to withstanding the test of time. He has already lived more than a century beyond his species’ 80-year average life expectancy—a feat that his safe environment, diet and medical care alone might not be able to explain.
In a new study published on Wednesday in Science Advances , researchers examined Jonathan’s DNA for genetic clues to his extraordinary age. To collect the data, Hollins propped Jonathan’s mouth open with a gloved finger and swabbed a sample of cheek cells and saliva.
“We almost never get to study an animal this old while it is still alive,” says co-author Steve Horvath , a biologist who studies aging at the University of California, Los Angeles, to the New York Times ’ Monique Brouillette.
Key context: False reports of Jonathan’s death
In April, false reports that Jonathan had died were circulated widely, stemming from a fake X post claiming to be the tortoise’s veterinarian. It turned out to be a hoax —a ploy for cryptocurrency donations.
The research team sequenced Jonathan’s DNA and identified 287 genetic variants that were unique to him. Many of these had to do with repairing damage to DNA, reducing inflammation and managing insulin. They also found that he shared aging-related genes with species including naked mole-rats , which almost never get cancer .
Additionally, they looked at Jonathan’s epigenome , the chemical tags on DNA that turn certain genes on and off. As organisms age, these switches become less predictable—tags might inconsistently attach or fall off, leading to erratic activity from genes. The team compared Jonathan’s epigenome with those of four younger tortoises.
Overall, Jonathan showed the chaos, or entropy, in the epigenome that would be expected for his age. But in the areas of the genome linked to things like DNA repair and mitochondria, the energy-producing centers in cells, Jonathan’s chemical tags were especially youthful. At these spots, Jonathan’s epigenome looked similar to DNA from a 5-year-old juvenile tortoise that the researchers studied.
The work doesn’t prove that these markers are the reason for Jonathan’s long life, but they offer a clue to how DNA might endure for long periods. They also align with findings from supercentenarians , humans who have lived to be more than 110 years old.
“Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face,” study co-author Stephen Clark , founder and chief scientist at the nonprofit Kallel Foundation for aging research, says in a statement . “Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people.”
But before any of this information can find a medical use, scientists will have to conduct deeper research. For one, Jonathan’s cheek swab contained incomplete DNA , so the team combined his genome with a younger tortoise’s DNA, resulting in a code that was only about 95 percent Jonathan—and allowing for the possibility that some of his unique DNA variants were not included in the sample. A blood test would have produced a full genome, but because of the risk of infection for the tortoise, Saint Helena officials did not allow it.
What’s more, Jonathan is just one study subject, and it’s difficult to generalize any results based on a lone individual. His genome was also compared against only a small handful of other tortoises, as bioinformatics researcher Kousuke Hashimoto of the University of Osaka, Japan, tells New Scientist ’s James Woodford, inviting the possibility that the other tortoises also had unique variants that were not identified. Nevertheless, he calls the study “fascinating.”
“The results integrate very well in the wider puzzle of what longevity is,” Björn Schumacher , who studies aging at the University of Cologne in Germany and was not involved in the study, tells the New York Times .
Jonathan was born in the Seychelles, an island nation in the Western Indian Ocean. But as a gift to the governor, he was brought to Saint Helena in 1882, when he was photographed as an adult. Since then, he has been living at Plantation House, the governor’s home, with other giant tortoises.
Hollins took charge of Jonathan’s care in 2009, when the animal was around 180 years old and not in great shape. Among markers of age, such as cataracts and a loss of smell that prevented him from finding his own food , the tortoise suffered from a soft beak that made it hard to graze. The veterinarian hand-fed Jonathan, who recovered and developed a razor-sharp edge to his beak within the next couple of years.
“He is symbolic of resilience, longevity, endurance,” Hollins tells Reuters ’ Marta Serafinko, “a persistent presence throughout huge historic events.”
Carlyn Kranking is Smithsonian magazine's associate web editor for science.

Europe has called on China to voluntarily reduce hybrid car exports into the continent, but authorities in Beijing had reportedly slapped down the request , according to the Financial Times.
The widening trade surplus between the EU and China has been a point of contention, with Germany and France previously having called on Brussels to develop a "last-resort" trade instrument to address imbalances.
Sefčovič said Friday that the final decision would still need Brussels' approval. Overall, he cast the two days of talks with China's Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Beijing as a positive first step, following a summer of rising tensions between China and the EU.
China's Commerce Ministry on Friday released a list of 16 "'consensus outcomes."
They included licenses for rare earth and permanent magnet export licenses to the EU. Sefcovic did not elaborate on a timeline for the rare earth exports.

articles.title_orig: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
articles.title_zh: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
articles.content_orig:
Pentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast live
US politics live – latest updates
The US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan .
The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December.
The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.
The plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media : “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”
Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted : “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”
Britain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”.
Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.”
Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth , according to the Pentagon.
Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes.
Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”
Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.
The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.
The execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by the US military since 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged.
Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following the botched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike last week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed.
Media have sought to televise US executions ⁠in the past, but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said.
Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan.
In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year.
Experts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly.
after newsletter promotion
The proposed live stream has prompted criticism from religious leaders. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.
Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said the plan was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”.
The Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes.
Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda.
Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations, posted on X : “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause.
“Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.”
Some experts have raised questions about whether the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death.
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” she told the Associated Press .
Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end.
“This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senseless pursuit of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.”
Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death.
It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.

articles.title_orig: Alleged Flydubai hijacker planned ‘suicide attack’ on Tel Aviv’s airport, early investigation finds
articles.title_zh: Alleged Flydubai hijacker planned ‘suicide attack’ on Tel Aviv’s airport, early investigation finds
articles.content_orig:
The alleged Flydubai hijacker had planned to crash the plane into Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv and was inspired by the 9/11 attacks, a preliminary investigation has found.
Hamam al-Hammami, the suspect in the hijacking attempt and co-pilot on board last week’s flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, wanted to carry out a similar attack to September 11, 2001, which led him to pursue an aviation career, according to a statement from the United Arab Emirates’ Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi shared by Emirati state media.
“The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his mind, which, according to his confessions, was connected to his decision to pursue a career in aviation,” Friday’s statement said. Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago, after four commercial planes were hijacked and crashed into three locations in the United States.
The co-pilot wanted to carry out “a premeditated plot with a terrorist objective, aimed at taking control of the aircraft and using it to carry out a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport,” with the aim of causing “the greatest possible number of casualties,” the statement added.
The early investigation also found that the September 30 flight was not al-Hammami’s first to Tel Aviv. He previously took part in two flights to Ben Gurion Airport to become familiar with the route and airport in preparation for the attack, the preliminary findings revealed.
An Israeli official and Israeli source familiar with the matter told CNN earlier that the alleged hijacker likely wanted to target the airport, the country’s main international gateway.
Al-Hammami, 29, was stopped by the actions of the captain and several passengers who restrained him and took back control of the airplane.
Al-Hammami became inclined toward extremism and terrorism in 2017 while he was studying in Australia, the investigation found. He was influenced by extremist publications he read and online content he followed that glorified terrorist groups and suicide attacks.
The statement said he “prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out his plot by increasing his exposure to material inciting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach.”
He previously worked for Oman Air from 2020 to 2024 before joining Royal Air Maroc in 2025, working at the Moroccan airline for several months before moving on to Flydubai in January 2026, the Emirati statement indicated.
A source told CNN earlier that the suspect was removed from flight training with Oman Air because of the concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at the Omani airline.
Alleged Flydubai hijacker said 9/11 attacks spurred him to become a pilot, early investigation finds
In a statement to Associated Press last week, Air Maroc said the suspect trained with the airline for three months in 2025 as part of the pre-employment process but he was not selected.
The UAE’s investigations also looked into Flydubai’s recruitment procedures for the suspect. Al-Hammami had met the professional and security requirements to be employed, the probe found, including holding a pilot’s license, a certificate of good conduct and completing the necessary exams.
There were “no indications emerging during those procedures that revealed his extremist inclinations or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot,” Attorney General Al Shamsi said, according to state media.
Al-Hammami told authorities he acted alone, though investigations into his claim are ongoing, the attorney general said.
Authorities are still investigating evidence, the possible involvement of others and is reviewing the recordings and technical reports, the according to Emirati state media.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's SpaceX just made a huge play to challenge the phone industry, and AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon stocks are getting crushed
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's SpaceX just made a huge play to challenge the phone industry, and AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon stocks are getting crushed
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) just sent a big message to the wireless industry: We want our piece of the subscriber pie.
Late Thursday, SpaceX said it will acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio. It positions Musk's satellite business Starlink to challenge legacy wireless giants across the US.
Shares of AT&T ( T ), T-Mobile ( TMUS ), and Verizon ( VZ ) tumbled on the news on Friday.
Concerns had already escalated across Wall Street that Starlink could disrupt legacy wireless operators like AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile by transitioning from a rural broadband service into a direct mobile competitor.
Following its strategic acquisition of terrestrial spectrum and rapid deployment of advanced satellites, SpaceX had laid the groundwork to launch its own standalone cellular network alongside its direct-to-cell capabilities.
SpaceX stock rose 1% on Friday.
The expansion threatens traditional carriers' high-margin enterprise, emergency service, and rural subscriber bases, as well as lucrative international roaming revenues.
AT&T CEO John Stankey has taken notice of Starlink's moves, but hasn't lost sleep over it… yet.
"I think they're going to find places where they clearly have a good solution," Stankey told Yahoo Finance at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia conference in September . "In airlines and flights today, they have a fantastic broadband solution. In rural parts or territories, it's a very efficient way to get good bandwidth to people. I think we see that there's going to be some IoT-type applications, like connecting vehicles that are largely outdoors and maybe have line of sight to the sky, that they're going to have an opportunity to go in and do some things there that maybe we haven't done as effectively."
While Starlink will present competition, Stankey added, "there's also going to be the complementary dynamic of us being able to solve that other 2% of the use cases I talked about and bring our customers to those satellite operators, whether it be Amazon or SpaceX. They'll be the beneficiary of us aggregating that traffic and bringing it into the wholesale market to be able to be used."

articles.title_orig: Europe’s Car Lobby Says EU-China Deal Can Ease Chinese Hybrid Surge ‘in Orderly Way’
articles.title_zh: Europe’s Car Lobby Says EU-China Deal Can Ease Chinese Hybrid Surge ‘in Orderly Way’
articles.content_orig:
Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs
The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.
The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.
“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.
China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.
Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.
He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.
“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.
“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart.
Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.
Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.
As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.
after newsletter promotion
China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.
The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.
A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.
It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.
While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

articles.title_orig: US diesel prices remain high despite Trump's moves to boost supplies
articles.title_zh: US diesel prices remain high despite Trump's moves to boost supplies
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Jarrett Renshaw and Nicole Jao
WASHINGTON/NEW YORK, Oct 9 (Reuters) - US diesel prices remain at near-record highs, up 70% since the US-Israeli war on Iran began despite two recent moves by President Donald Trump to boost supplies: pressuring allies to release emergency reserves and ‌expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel.
The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered a severe global fuel supply crunch, pushing the average ‌US diesel price to $6.28 a gallon on Friday, according to motorist group AAA.
"Aside from a recession that hammers consumption, the only thing that can prevent oil prices from rising further and ​put them on a sharp downward trajectory is a durable end to conflicts in the Arabian Gulf and between Russia and Ukraine," said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy Group. "Otherwise, policy options range from marginal to counterproductive."
High fuel prices have made it harder for Trump and his Republican Party to defend narrow congressional majorities in the November 3 midterm elections. The cost of living is the top item cited by voters in a Reuters/Ipsos poll, and high diesel prices put particular ‌pressure on traditional Republican constituencies: farmers, truckers and rural ⁠voters.
Trump's approval rating is at a career-low 32%, according to the poll.
The administration has touted a G7 agreement to release 100 million barrels of oil and petroleum products as a major step to help ease prices, but those barrels ⁠appear to largely cover what remains of a March emergency release by International Energy Agency members, rather than new supply.
A White House official disputed that characterization, saying the earlier commitments were not specifically for refined products. The administration negotiated for the previously committed barrels to be front-loaded with diesel and released on a tight timeline beginning ​immediately, ​the official said.
The White House said Trump was focused on easing temporary disruptions while pursuing ​longer-term energy policies.
The administration's other major initiative, an executive ‌order allowing red-dyed diesel on public roads through year-end, has drawn limited industry uptake. The fuel is chemically identical to what trucks normally burn but is tinted to show it is exempt from the 24.4-cent-per-gallon federal highway tax.
The order defers the federal tax and waives penalties for burning off-road fuel on highways. But major retailers and marketers remain wary of selling it because of unclear tax liabilities, logistical hurdles and the risk of fines when trucks cross state lines.
The tax savings are relatively small with diesel prices above $6 a gallon.
David Fialkov, who lobbies on behalf of NATSO, a trade group for truck stops ‌and travel centers, said the White House appeared to be encouraging the supply chain to ​sell dyed fuel through channels not traditionally used for highway diesel, but said that most ​reputable retailers and marketers were unlikely to do so.
John Tirado, president ​of New Jersey-based commercial fuel supplier Summa Energy, called the red-dyed diesel plan "a Band-Aid on a much bigger problem."
The White ‌House said more than 4,000 retailers distribute dyed diesel. It ​said Treasury Department guidance will clarify the ​rules, allowing drivers to use it without federal tax or penalty. It said the savings should outweigh any detour costs for truckers seeking the fuel.
"The fundamental problem facing the US is not taxation but an exceptionally tight global market for refined products," said Caspian Conran, lead economist ​at Baringa, citing disruptions to energy flows from the ‌Middle East and reduced refining output elsewhere.
He described the measures as short-term steps ahead of the election that could provide "probably a few ​weeks of relief," rather than a durable solution.
(Reporting By Jarrett Renshaw in Washington, Additional reporting by Nicole Jao in New York ​and Timothy Gardner in Washington; Editing by Nathan Crooks, David Gregorio, Rod Nickel)

articles.title_orig: One World Community Health Center hosts free health fair in Omaha
articles.title_zh: One World Community Health Center hosts free health fair in Omaha
articles.content_orig:
By Hannah Nazarenus , News intern
Oct. 9, 2026, 10:48 a.m. ·
One World Community Health Center will host a free, family-friendly health fair Saturday at the South Omaha Campus of Metropolitan Community College as part of Binational Health Week.
The event is open to anyone, regardless of insurance status or whether they are a One World patient, said Vivian Garcia, outreach manager at One World. The fair runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
“Right now, we can see that there's a lot of families that are struggling to even cover that extra cost that insurance doesn't cover,” Garcia said. “So that’s the reason why we invite everyone. It doesn't matter if you have health insurance, if you don't have health insurance.”
Garcia said they expect more than 400 people, up from last year, when attendance was still recovering after COVID-19 forced the events to pause.
“It’s not about getting more patients for a clinic,” Garcia said. “It’s about getting these resources and getting education out in a community.”
Visitors can get cholesterol, blood sugar and blood pressure checks. Specialty services include dermatology, hearing and vision screenings, and basic dental screenings for adults and children. This will be the first year the fair offers ear cleanings for people who fail the hearing test.
Vision services have drawn the most interest, Garcia said. This is the second year the fair will offer full vision screenings with glasses prescribed on site.
“The only thing that they're going to be asked is a good address to have those glasses sent over to their home,” Garcia said.
More than 200 people received glasses that way last year.
Garcia said the fair connects attendees to One World and other clinics and organizations in the Omaha area. Participants fill out a short form with no identifying information.
“What we also hear a lot is just navigating the healthcare system overall,” Garcia said. “Knowing how to go into a provider, to the clinic, to set up an initial appointment. Sometimes individuals are maybe just arriving here in Nebraska, and they don't know exactly where to go.”
Binational Health Week is an initiative of the Mexican government, and One World coordinates its events with the Mexican consulate.
The Saturday fair is the last of three October events. One World also held one Oct. 3 at All Care Health Center in Council Bluffs, Iowa, and a women’s night offering breast exams and cancer screenings in partnership with UNMC.
More information on the event and others hosted by One World can be found on its website.

articles.title_orig: Moderna stock jumps on planned national cancer vaccine effort
articles.title_zh: Moderna stock jumps on planned national cancer vaccine effort
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Moderna ( MRNA ) stock popped 9% on Friday after the New York Times reported new details about an effort to accelerate cancer vaccine development. Investors saw the mRNA biotech company, in particular, as a beneficiary.
Other pharmaceutical stocks, including Pfizer ( PFE ), BioNTech ( BNTX ), and Merck ( MRK ), also rose.
According to the New York Times, the new initiative is a public-private partnership — similar to the effort that produced COVID-19 vaccines — that involves the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the NIH's nonprofit arm, researchers, pharmaceutical and biotech companies, advocacy groups, other nonprofits, and patients.
Stacey Adam, a senior clinical officer at the NIH's foundation, told the New York Times that she expects the program to launch in December. In 2024, the UK launched a similar program, called the Cancer Vaccine Launch Pad .
Moderna is viewed as a leader in mRNA cancer treatments. The stock soared in August on positive results for a melanoma treatment , developed with Merck.
Year to date, Moderna stock is up 627%.

articles.title_orig: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay.
articles.title_zh: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay.
articles.content_orig:
The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African legal pioneer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for defending international law and institutions in a world in which increasingly “might overtakes right.”
Pillay, 85, has a decadeslong career that spans defending Nelson Mandela and standing up against the racist apartheid regime in South Africa, to leading a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
“Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
Frydnes contrasted Pillay’s work with the wider international “shift towards power politics,” in which “international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack.”
Her “distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law,” he said. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”
Pillay learned of her prize at the Nuremberg Forum, an international law gathering in Germany. She told an applauding crowd, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” prompting laughter.
That was a reference to President Donald Trump’s long-standing ambitions to win the Nobel Peace Prize, and the offer by last year’s winner, Maria Corina Machado, to share it with him as she sought support for her efforts in Venezuela.
“Everybody asks me: ‘When are you going to stop? When are you going to stop?’” Pillay said , adding that despite turning 85 last month, she had no intention of doing so.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza, namely what’s happening there is genocide,” she said.
“One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage,” she added. “But why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law and you look at all the facts.”
In later more formal remarks accepting the prize, she dedicated the award to “all of the survivors of international crimes,” warning against efforts “which attempt to weaken international criminal justice” which “risk returning us to a world in which power, rather than law, determines whose suffering matters.”
Among her many positions, Pillay previously served as a judge on the International Criminal Court , a frequent focus of ire for the Trump administration. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced fresh sanctions on the body on Friday, hours after the prize was announced.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” Rubio said in a statement, threatening to continue a campaign “to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick.”
Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, was with Pillay in Germany and among the first people to congratulate her on the prize.
“This could not be a better choice at a time of attacks against international justice,” Callamard told NBC News. “She is a former ICC judge at a time when the U.S. administration is seeking to destroy the ICC,” she said, praising her work leading the U.N. commission “which found that Israel committed the crime of genocide at a time when many states are trying to defend and protect Israel’s actions.”
The ICC condemned the new U.S. sanctions Friday, and separately praised Pillay’s win as “an important recognition of the vital role that international justice plays as a cornerstone of lasting peace.”
Pillay was not among those speculated to be front-runners, who included Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of anti-Kremlin figure Alexei Navalny, Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate, and Mykola Kuleba , who founded an organization to rescue Ukrainian children abducted and forcibly taken to Russia.
The Norwegian Nobel Institute said it had has registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s peace prize, with politicians, international judges and professors among those who can put names forward. The committee that decides the winner is composed of five members appointed by the Norwegian Parliament.
The leaders of Israel, Pakistan and Cambodia all said they nominated Trump for the prize, though he said this week he didn’t think he would win.
“I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Wednesday. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.”
Trump did not congratulate Pillay on Friday. Instead, on Truth Social, he reposted a message from another user that said the Nobel committee had “shamed itself beyond repair and demeaned the once great Nobel Peace Prize,” describing Pillay as “an unabashed hater of America and Israel.”
Alexander Smith is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital based in London.

articles.title_orig: China and Europe Step Back From Trade War With Limits on Chinese Car Exports
articles.title_zh: China and Europe Step Back From Trade War With Limits on Chinese Car Exports
articles.content_orig:
The agreement will see Chinese hybrid vehicle exports decline by ‘several million cars’ in the coming years, EU trade chief says
The European Union and China have “reached an understanding” that will cut Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc by “more than a half”, in a temporary salve to trade tensions that have threatened to boil over into a full-blown trade war.
Speaking after marathon trade talks in Beijing, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said the deal would see China slash its hybrid car exports “by several million cars” over a four-year period.
“This is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tensions, and I very much appreciate that,” Sefcovic told reporters in the Chinese capital.
The sides also agreed to expedite EU applications for rare earth mineral export licences and improve market access for goods including car parts, olive oil and textiles, which Sefcovic said could be worth “almost €4 billion” (US$4.5 billion) in current export value.

articles.title_orig: Get in the Spotlight With the Line Life Podcast
articles.title_zh: Get in the Spotlight With the Line Life Podcast
articles.content_orig:
A few years ago, I partnered with Danielle Blanchette and our team from T&D World to launch the  Line Life Podcast. Our mission was simple: to bring the stories from the pages of T&D World magazine to the airwaves.
Due to the nature of their jobs, lineworkers are not in an office working behind a computer day in and day out. Instead, they are slipping on their work boots, packing their tool bags and heading out in the field to keep the power flowing to the customers in their service territories.
Because lineworkers spend a lot of time traveling from one location to the next in their bucket trucks, we wanted to give them a way to listen to our field-focused Electric Utility Operations (EUO) stories on the go.
We started with only audio stories, and then we started branching out into interview-style episodes. For the last few years, I've recorded interviews with lineworkers and their loved ones for future episodes of the Line Life Podcast.
With the 2026 International Lineman's Rodeo Week only a few days away, we're excited to offer that opportunity again to the Lineman's Rodeo attendees. Swing by the T&D World Booth #001 (in the breezeway between the ballroom and the exhibit hall) to sit down with me, Amy Fischbach, for a conversation about your career in the line trade.
I air interview-style episodes on the first and third Fridays of each month and audio stories on the second and fourth Fridays on Podbean and in your favorite podcasting app.
To see all the episodes we've recorded over the years, go to linelife.podbean.com . You can also check out our new International Lineman's Rodeo Roundup page on our T&D World website to see the past Rodeo-related episodes.
I look forward to seeing you during the 2026 International Lineman's Rodeo and putting you in the spotlight for the Line Life Podcast!
Amy Fischbach is the Head of Content for T&D World magazine and manages the Electric Utility Operations section. She is the host of the Line Life Podcast , which celebrates the grit, courage and inspirational teamwork of the line trade.  She also works on the annual Lineworker Supplement and the Vegetation Management Supplement as well as the Lineman Life and Lineman's Rodeo News enewsletters. Amy also covers events such as the Trees & Utilities conference and the International Lineman's Rodeo. She is the past president of the ASBPE Educational Foundation and ASBPE and earned her bachelor's and master's degrees in journalism from Kansas State University. articles.title_orig: ICE officer shoots man in New York City
articles.title_zh: ICE officer shoots man in New York City
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Conservative commentator Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary
An ICE officer shot a man in New York City on Thursday as the man’s 5-year-old child was in the car, officials said, prompting anger from protesters and the city’s mayor, who called it “an outrage.”
The shooting happened at around 4 p.m. during a “targeted enforcement operation,” the Department of Homeland Security said, as federal officers were seeking a “criminal illegal alien from the Dominican Republic” who had a prior conviction for grand larceny.
“During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured,” the department said, without naming the victim.
The man who was shot was identified as Oscar Belgal, 28, according to the New York Police Department, four law enforcement sources and past court records.
At least one ICE agent fired seven rounds, and the man was struck in the neck, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference Thursday night, as protesters shouted nearby.
The injured man was taken by the NYPD to a hospital in stable condition after the shooting, she said.
An NYPD surveillance camera captured part of the encounter but not the shooting, Tisch said.
The video shows the person who was shot backing into a parking space; then, one plainclothes federal law enforcement officer approaches the driver’s side with a gun drawn, and a second officer approaches by the driver’s side headlight, the commissioner said.
“The vehicle then starts to move forward and goes out of camera view,” Tisch said.
That car was later found with gunshot damage to the front windshield and the back window shattered, and an ICE vehicle was found with damage to its left front panel, and a lower panel disconnected, she added.
Bystander video recorded of the aftermath shows the wounded man sitting on the ground in handcuffs and talking to officers.
Mamdani says shooting of man by ICE was ‘an outrage’
Two 911 calls were made about shots fired, and a federal agent called 911 requesting the fire department and then the NYPD, Tisch said.
NYPD officers responding to an unrelated call in the area also heard the shots and responded, the commissioner said.
“When they arrived, they encountered several men in various forms of attire, including some in construction-style vests, face masks and at least one carrying a long gun,” Tisch said.
The shot person was handcuffed and seated on the ground, she said. He had been shot in the neck below the left ear, she added.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned ICE as “rotten to its core” and said the agency, which has been criticized for tactics and immigration crackdowns under the Trump administration, has been acting with impunity.
“There is no explanation for these tactics. There is no explanation for federal officers firing this many rounds into a car that has a 5-year-old in the car,” Mamdani said. “There is no explanation.”
Mamdani said the man’s child was in the back seat and physically unharmed.
The shooting happened in the Marble Hill neighborhood of Upper Manhattan, near the Bronx, Mamdani said. He described it as a residential area.
“We are right there by a subway, and the pretext of ICE is, in their words, to keep this country safe,” Mamdani said. “How is it keeping anyone safe to have, as you just heard from the police commissioner, individuals wearing construction vests and masks with long guns?”
“Residents have no idea if these are law enforcement agents or if they are simply attacking someone on the street,” he said.
The person who was shot had two prior arrests in New York City, Tisch said. One, in 2023, was for robbery; he pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years probation, she said.
The other was for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025, and that case is still pending, she said.
DHS said that the man who was shot has associations to the Trinitarios gang.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she spoke with Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the shooting Thursday evening, urging them to halt ICE enforcement operations in the state.
“I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth,” she said .
Phil Helsel is a reporter for NBC News.
Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Samantha Cookinham is an NBC News assignment editor.

articles.title_orig: Apple ‘Welcome home’ event: Three new products are coming next week
articles.title_zh: Apple ‘Welcome home’ event: Three new products are coming next week
articles.content_orig:
Apple officially confirmed yesterday that it will hold a product launch event next week on October 13. With a “Welcome home” tagline, the launch is expected to focus on new smart home products. Here’s everything to expect at next week’s Apple event.
9to5Mac’s Apple event coverage is supported by Sony : Shop Sony’s huge Amazon sale to score big savings on its entire TV lineup, including models with Apple AirPlay 2 support.
There are two components to the event, as Ryan outlined . There is the in-person experience for members of the press in New York City, as well as what Mark Gurman has called an “online video presentation.”
This suggests we can expect press releases and a video (or videos) to drop around 9 a.m. ET/6 a.m. PT on October 13. Apple hasn’t confirmed this, so the actual launch might vary. At a minimum, though, we know it will announce something on October 13, and some people will see it in person while the rest of us follow along from home.
Next week’s headlining announcement will be Apple’s long-rumored smart display product, which we’ve been calling the “HomePad.” Apple believes that this product can serve as a central hub for your house, powered by Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.
According to Bloomberg , the device will have a 6-inch square display atop a half-dome base, with a metal arm holding it up. The HomePad will reportedly come in two variations: one that can be mounted on a wall and one that can sit on a countertop. Reports have likened the design to Apple’s iconic iMac G4 .
One of the flagship features of the HomePad will be its ability to recognize multiple people in a household. Mark Gurman reports that it can recognize who is talking to it or approaching it and dynamically adjust what’s shown on the screen.
In terms of software , the HomePad reportedly mixes different elements of the Apple Watch, Apple TV, and iPad. This includes iPad-like app designs and Apple Watch-style icons. It will also heavily borrow from the iPhone for widgets and StandBy mode .
Apple is also expected to announce a new Apple TV 4K next week, its first update to the set-top box since November 2022. The new Apple TV will look the same as its predecessor, but it will reportedly include the A19 or A19 Pro chip.
That upgraded chip will allow Apple to bring Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features to the Apple TV for the first time.
Apple is also reportedly working on new software features for the Apple TV and HomePod. For example, there are code references to a new feature that would let you arrange four full-sized HomePods in a surround sound system when paired with Apple TV.
The HomePod mini will also get its first proper upgrade next week. The big change here will be a new chip that is much faster than the current model’s S5 processor, bringing support for Siri AI. For context, the S5 chip used in the current HomePod mini is the same chip Apple debuted with the Apple Watch Series 5.
Beyond the faster chip, the new HomePod mini 2 will reportedly come in new colors:
Finally, Apple is working with LG on new “second-party” accessories for HomeKit. Apple reportedly collaborated with LG to co-develop products including a smart lock, thermostat, doorbell, and multiple cameras.
Bloomberg says Apple won’t release these accessories for “at least a few more months.” They could still be shown off as part of Apple’s broader home strategy next week, though.
While we obviously have a pretty good idea of what Apple will announce next week thanks to these rumors, I’m still really excited to see the company unveil its home roadmap. It’s felt like a category Apple has neglected for far too long, and one it might finally start taking seriously next week.
What are you most excited to see at Apple’s “Welcome home” event next week? Are you planning to buy the all-new HomePad or upgrade your Apple TV and HomePod mini? Let us know down in the comments.
