articles.title_orig: World Bank and IMF’s lack of climate action could make countries bystanders in their own destruction
articles.title_zh: World Bank and IMF’s lack of climate action could make countries bystanders in their own destruction
articles.content_orig:
© World Economic Forum / Benedikt von Loebell
The World Bank and IMF are shifting away from explicit climate action towards resilience, reflecting political pressure from the US that weakens their response to global heating, argues Federico Sibaja  and Jon Sward.
The authors criticise the World Bank’s approach after its financing supported a Nepal hydropower project that was damaged by devastating floods despite warnings and the absence of a proper climate-risk assessment.
Meanwhile, IMF-backed austerity and fossil-fuel policies in countries including Ecuador and Pakistan are limiting investment in climate adaptation and, in some cases, undermining the shift to renewable energy.
With climate-vulnerable countries facing mounting damage, the authors argue that institutions must expand grant-based finance and debt relief, and ensure climate risks are built into lending decisions and economic programmes.
In a recent interview with the New York Times , World Bank President Ajay Banga explained that the bank wants to avoid the “emotional” debate around climate change and instead focus on resilient investments.
For the leader of an institution that describes itself as the “knowledge bank”, such a desire to skirt the realities of climate science is of course the result of political calculus.
The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, has also shifted gears in recent years: she went from calling for an end to “business as usual” at COP28 , to agreeing with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the need to refocus away from climate change. She has also cut the budget earmarked for climate work by 27%.
Meanwhile, Bessent has questioned the cause of global warming and referred to climate action at global financial institutions as driven by “elite beliefs” .
The World Bank and IMF’s change in approach comes as no surprise, as there is a potentially steep cost of them falling afoul of their largest shareholder, amid its wider war on multilateralism.
But what’s been less discussed is the wider cost of the Bretton Woods institutions’ failure to act in the midst of an accelerating climate emergency – of which the serious flooding in Bangkok, where the World Bank and IMF convene their annual meetings next week, is a stark reminder.
After a prolonged debate on the future of the bank’s climate commitments in the Spring, a compromise was reached in June , when it extended its climate change action plan (CCAP) “indefinitely”, but retired its 45% climate finance target.
As the US’s anti-climate action agenda has cast a long shadow at the institution and elsewhere since last year, bank officials increasingly say their goal is to deliver resilient investments, echoing Banga’s recent statements.
However, there are serious questions about whether the bank’s approach is advancing its aim.
The recent flood disaster in Nepal, which killed more than 1,450 people (with around 5,800 still missing), also damaged 13 hydropower projects, including the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower plant. Alongside other lenders , Trishuli was backed by financing from the World Bank’s private investment arm , IFC, and a US$87.4mn guarantee from its political risk arm, MIGA. Yet, despite repeated warnings from an independent expert panel, no climate and disaster risk assessment had been properly undertaken as of 2024.
The World Bank needs to ensure that “resilience” is more than an empty signifier. This means having mechanisms in place across all lending instruments to evaluate whether its actions are genuinely leading to positive outcomes for people and the planet, including ex-post assessments of projects that emphasise learning from past mistakes.
It also means rethinking the the bank’s neoliberal era loan conditions in its policy based lending , which have promoted wholesale privatisation in key sectors like energy, and ensuring countries have the policy and fiscal space to pursue green industrial policy .
As evidenced by the Nepal crisis, with the country facing an estimated US$4.7bn in reconstruction costs, climate-vulnerable countries also urgently need a rapid scaling up of grant-based climate finance and debt relief . The World Bank could use its convening role to help move this discussion forward.
The IMF’s relevance has grown due to increasingly frequent shocks to the global economy, such as spikes in fossil fuel prices and extreme weather events. In July 2026 , 30 countries were implementing IMF programmes with conditionalities, and 14 other countries were seeking new arrangements.
Recent analysis has shown that its programmes’ reliance on fiscal consolidation and foreign exchange accumulation can undermine countries’ climate policy goals and put macroeconomic stability – Bessent’s  “focus” of the IMF – at risk. So, while the IMF has become better at diagnosing climate risk, it is also exacerbating it.
For example, in Ecuador, the IMF-backed programme requires primary adjustment of 6.6% of GDP. Such fiscal adjustment can make it harder to invest in climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure. At the same time, the programme explicitly aims to increase oil output.
The same goes for Pakistan. The country has been on the frontlines of the climate crisis in the last few years, with devastating floods in 2022. Yet IMF-backed fiscal consolidation has constrained spending at a time when the country faces enormous adaptation needs. Moreover, reforms in fiscal policy are undermining the energy transition: due to IMF-led energy subsidy removal and tariff increases, the country began a rapid shift to solar, only to see it undermined by IMF-backed higher taxes on solar panels.
Back in June, the IMF’s own independent evaluation office flagged this contradiction. It identified the review of progam design and conditionality , the process through which the institution evaluates the performance of its lending programmes and agrees ways to improve them, as a chance to address it. Yet, when the review wrapped up last month, climate was firmly excluded .
As more countries turn to the IMF to address their vulnerability to shocks, its push for fiscal adjustment and commodity extraction risks accelerating that same vulnerability.
At the upcoming annual meetings, we need to see serious efforts to resolve this contradiction. A good place to start would be the guidance the IMF provides to staff designing loan programmes, which will be developed in the next few months. This must clearly outline under what circumstances climate goals are central to programme success and cannot be ignored.
Without a change of course, the IMF and World Bank will miss a key window of opportunity to stem a runaway climate crisis. In the present context, delaying action is just another form of climate denial.
This page was last updated October 9, 2026
Federico Sibaja is the lead for Fair International Financial System work at Recourse. An economist from the Universidad de Buenos Aires, he is an expert on the interactions between debt and climate policy. He has extensive experience in policymaking, research and campaigning across Argentina, Belgium and internationally.
Jon Sward is environment project manager at the Bretton Woods Project, where he oversees its climate advocacy work towards the World Bank and the IMF. He holds a PhD from the School of Global Studies at the University of Sussex.

articles.title_orig: PEI Group reveals the world's 100 biggest private markets firms have raised $5.74 trillion in five years
articles.title_zh: PEI Group reveals the world's 100 biggest private markets firms have raised $5.74 trillion in five years
articles.content_orig:
PEI Group's ground-breaking Private Markets 100 report measures private equity, real estate, infrastructure, private credit and secondaries together for the first time.
LONDON , Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The 100 largest private markets managers raised $5.74 trillion between 2021 and 2025, more than the annual economic output of Germany*, according to the inaugural Private Markets 100 published by PEI Group.
Blackstone heads the ranking at $356.7 billion, KKR is second at $302.2 billion and Goldman Sachs Alternatives third at $215.3 billion.
The top 10 raised $2.04 trillion between them, 35.5 percent of the total.
PEI Private Markets 100 top 10
Goldman Sachs Alternatives
Brookfield Asset Management
The specialist is disappearing
PEI Group is the first business intelligence firm to provide a five-year global fundraising ranking across the five major asset classes, bringing together data from PEI's well-known industry standard rankings which investors trust and rely on.
Measuring the five asset classes together in this way shows what separate rankings cannot: the biggest managers are no longer single asset class specialists.
Sixteen of the top 100 firms in the ranking raised money across all five strategies, and seven of the top 10 are active in all five, while a quarter of the list (25 firms) made the top 100 by being active in a single asset class.
Ares Management shows the largest shift in a single year. It raised more private credit than any other firm, moved from 10 th to fourth in real estate and from 16 th to 10 th in secondaries. Added together, that makes it the fifth-largest private markets fundraiser in the world, ahead of both Brookfield and BlackRock.
Much of the convergence is being bought rather than built. In the past two years KKR has acquired sports investor Arctos Partners, EQT has acquired secondaries firm Coller Capital for up to $3.7 billion, and Goldman Sachs has bought Industry Ventures. General Atlantic has acquired infrastructure manager Actis and BNP Paribas has completed its purchase of AXA Investment Managers.
"The industry has outgrown its own categories," said Dan Gunner, Director of Research at PEI Group . "Firms that were buyout houses 10 years ago now raise more for credit than for equity. By methodically analysing and launching the first ever PEI Private Markets 100, we are offering a complete view of the wider market which allows the industry to see the full fundraising picture like never before. This is testimony to the unmatched capability we bring in Research and Analysis, and the breadth and depth of the data we have across private markets, which stretches back over more than 15 years."
* Germany nominal GDP, 2025 $5.01trn (IMF World Economic Outlook, Oct 2025)
Understanding the PEI Private Markets 100
The PEI Private Markets 100 ranks managers by capital raised for private markets funds over the five years to 31 December 2025. It consolidates PEI Group's six established asset class rankings, each compiled annually from manager submissions and validated against public filings, regulatory disclosures and fund documentation. A manager needed $18.97 billion to make the list. Figures are amounts raised, not assets under management. Where a fund invests across strategies its capital is split between rankings rather than counted twice.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices fall as Trump pauses Iran attacks, China restarts fuel exports – business live
articles.title_zh: Oil prices fall as Trump pauses Iran attacks, China restarts fuel exports – business live
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Thursday, as Iran ramped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and Hurricane Isaias threatened U.S. offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, gained 4% to close at $104.28 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 3.6% to settle at $91.49 per barrel.
Nine tankers have come under attack in and around Hormuz over the past week, jeopardizing the recent recovery in crude oil flows through the strait
Oil prices backed off session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. NBC News, citing unnamed sources, reported earlier that Trump and his national security team were considering renewing strikes in the coming weeks.
Some 9.5 million barrels per day exited Hormuz during the week ended Tuesday, about 30% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to Kpler data. Crude flows from the Middle East, including pipeline workarounds, stood at 16.4 million bpd which is nearly equivalent to prewar levels.
In the Gulf of Mexico, oil companies have shut in about 500,000 bpd, or 25% of offshore production in the region, as Hurricane Isaias churns toward the coasts of Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida panhandle.
Tensions are sharply escalating in the Middle East. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen fired missiles at airports in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and the city of Abha on Tuesday and Wednesday. Three people died and 36 were injured, according to the state-owned media outlet Al Arabiya.
The Saudis intercepted another volley of ballistic missiles fired Thursday at Riyadh and Khamis Mushait, a spokesperson for the kingdom's military said.
"While flows from the region have largely normalized, the need for US navy escorts, increased costs and logistical frictions and constant risk of being attacked call into question the longer-term feasibility of the flows," said Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"This ultimately warrants a sticky risk premium to remain in pricing," McKay told clients in a Thursday note.

articles.title_orig: What Smart People Say About PERM Suspension on Microsoft and Indian Tech
articles.title_zh: What Smart People Say About PERM Suspension on Microsoft and Indian Tech
articles.content_orig:
For foreign workers at some of the biggest employers in tech, there's another twist in an already uncertain system.
The Trump administration’s decision to suspend Microsoft, Adobe, and other named tech companies from the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program has renewed debate over whether stricter skilled-immigration policies protect American workers or hurt American businesses.
On Thursday morning, Vice President JD Vance announced the suspension at a press conference. He singled out Microsoft , saying: "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants."
PERM is not a visa. It is the Labor Department certification employers generally need before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card. Vance said that some companies had abused the system and used foreign workers to undercut Americans.
In a statement on Thursday, Microsoft disputed Vance's accusations, saying most of its H-1B filings were for existing employees rather than new hires.
"Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people," the company wrote.
The action also affects six major IT services companies with deep ties to India’s tech sector: Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, and Capgemini.
Here’s what immigration-policy experts and Indian tech voices are saying:
"Technology companies depend heavily on the 'H-1B-to-green-card' pipeline to retain specialized foreign talent," Hector Chichoni, a partner at the business law firm Greenspoon Marder, told Business Insider.
"With the PERM process effectively frozen, affected companies cannot move employees forward toward permanent residence , making them vulnerable to the loss of critical talent, either to employers not subject to the suspension or through employees returning to their home countries," he added.
Chichoni said the affected IT companies are likely to "vigorously defend themselves" against the allegations the government has made.
The decision also will have a particularly significant impact on Indian tech professionals who are already facing decades-long green card backlogs , Chichoni said.
Hira, a Howard University political science professor and a longtime critic of the H-1B program, called the move against Microsoft “very significant.”
Hira has long argued that employers can use the program in ways that depress pay and disadvantage US workers. He told the Associated Press on Thursday that there are supposed to be protections requiring employers to show that hiring an H-1B worker does not hurt similarly employed Americans.
“That’s never been enforced,” Hira said.
Rand, a former senior advisor at US Citizenship and Immigration Services during the Biden administration, took the opposite view. He called Vance’s announcement “incoherent” in a statement to AP.
Rand’s argument is that the policy could worsen the problem Vance says he wants to solve. H-1B workers are generally tied to their employers for their immigration status. A green card gives workers far more freedom to switch jobs and bargain over pay.
“If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are ‘indentured servants,’ then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards,” Rand told AP.
Pai, an India-based vice president of investments at the country's largest brokerage Zerodha, reacted to what a more restrictive US path to permanent residency could mean for India.
In a statement on X, Pai wrote that the immediate downside could be fewer high-earning Indians in the US, which in turn could mean lower remittances, less soft power, and less angel investments flowing back into Indian startups. He also noted that India receives roughly $125 billion in annual remittances, with the US accounting for about a quarter of that total.
But he also saw a potential upside. If US companies cannot bring talent to America, he wrote, “they probably will bring the work to India.”
US visa uncertainty may also keep more top engineers in India to build domestic companies and AI startups, he added.
Nasscom, India's main tech industry group, said immigration policy and skilled-talent mobility should be treated as separate issues.
"While the decision affects a specific immigration pathway, Nasscom has consistently maintained that immigration and skilled talent mobility are two distinct issues and should not be viewed through the same lens," the group said in a statement to local media
It also said the number of employees moving from H-1B status to permanent residency through PERM is “relatively limited.”

articles.title_orig: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.title_zh: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.content_orig:
Singapore, one of the wealthiest cities in the world, has become the most polluted on the planet as it chokes under a blanket of thick, toxic smog caused by fires in neighboring Indonesia.
Pollution has cast a pall on the city-state as it gets ready to host a packed weekend of marquee events ranging from international conferences to the glitzy Formula One Grand Prix night race.
Air quality in the city-state was at the “very unhealthy” range with an air quality index (AQI) of 216 Friday mid-morning, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir.
The financial hub topped the list of most polluted cities by IQAir this week and was still at the top spot Friday morning. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected by the Indonesian fires, was at number two.
Singapore’s skyline, including Marina Bay Sands and other skyscrapers were reduced to faint silhouettes amid the pollution.
The key Asian financial hub – with a population of 6.21 million and annual GDP of more than $650 billion – and neighboring Malaysia have had to endure the haze almost annually.
Fires in Indonesia are an annual event during the country’s dry season when huge stretches of peatland are cleared and drained for commercial plantations, including those that produce palm oil, an ingredient used in a slew of products from noodles to toothpaste.
But this year, the arrival of what’s expected to be a “super” El Niño — a supercharged version of the natural climate pattern which tends to bring bone dry conditions to the country — has set the stage for unusually intense blazes.
In an update on its website Thursday, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said “moderate to dense smoke plumes from southern and central Sumatra and West Kalimantan were observed to drift towards Singapore,” referring to Indonesian regions.
“Under the prevailing southeasterly or southerly winds, smoke haze may continue to drift towards Singapore,” it added.
Entertainment events held outdoors at the F1 event in Singapore could potentially be affected but not the race itself, the motorsport’s governing FIA said Thursday, according to Reuters. On Friday, race organizer Singapore GP told CNN “there are currently no plans to modify our entertainment activities” at the event.
Acts to entertain F1 spectators include Janet Jackson and The Killers, among others.
This is not the first time the Singapore night race is facing air quality issues. The races in 2015 and 2019 were also enveloped in thick haze and they went ahead.
Nevertheless, the Singapore Tourism Board told CNN on Friday: “Action plans are in place based on the intensity of the haze.”
F1 drivers, however, don’t seem too bothered. Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas, who cycled more than 400km (248 miles) from Malaysia to Singapore this week, told Reuters: “I don’t feel like it’s that extreme yet. I mean, it’s not great, but I don’t think there’s that much you can do.”
Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton told Reuters he has “much bigger issues to focus on.”
Neighboring Malaysia has also been heavily affected by the smog with the education ministry shutting schools across several states this week as the situation worsens.
Laura Paddison contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt
articles.content_orig:
Attorneys for Christa Pike hold a news conference after a judge ruled the Tennessee Department of Corrections must preserve all evidence related to the failed execution of Pike, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Christa Pike has begun walking and eating again at a hospital a week after surviving Tennessee's attempt to execute her with lethal drugs, her attorneys said Thursday.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to giver her a lethal injection eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn't kill her, and her arms were left burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator.
Her first steps on Wednesday were "limited" and she required some assistance as she walked on Thursday, her lawyers said in a statement. She is also regaining mobility in her arms, and she was able to eat for the first time.
But the lawyers warned uncertainty remains about her physical recovery and her legal standing after the attempt to carry out her death sentence.
The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty. Texas on Wednesday carried out the first execution in the U.S. since the Tennessee attempt.
"While her physical recovery has been remarkable, significant questions remain about the long-term effects of what she endured," her attorneys said in Thursday's statement. "Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die."
Pike regained consciousness Tuesday and was able to speak after awakening, they said.
They initially described her as "confused" soon after regaining consciousness, and said Thursday that she continued to struggle with concentration and memory. Doctors say it is too early to assess the long-term impacts, the attorneys added.
It also remains unclear whether Tennessee will try to execute her again. Her attorneys have said that they will urge Republican Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without parole.
"She should never be subjected to another execution attempt," they said in the statement.
Luke Ihnen, attorney for Christa Pike, speaks during a news conference after a judge ruled the Tennessee Department of Corrections must preserve all evidence related to the failed execution of Pike, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
Lee has since postponed the state's only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of why the execution failed. The state's prison chief resigned after the execution attempt.
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream.
Pike's attorneys wrote in a court filing that "apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed."
State officials have offered no explanation of what occurred.
As the process got underway Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital.

articles.title_orig: Museum honours two key World War Two RAF stations
articles.title_zh: Museum honours two key World War Two RAF stations
articles.content_orig:
A museum has paid tribute to two former RAF stations that played vital roles in Bomber Command operations during World War Two.
The RAF Witchford and Mepal Museum has opened on Lancaster Way Business Park in Ely, Cambridgeshire, to show the contribution RAF Witchford and RAF Mepal made to the Lancaster bombers' offensive.
Grovemere Property bought RAF Witchford from the Ministry of Defence after the war and redeveloped the site.
"It really is just amazing that we are now home to all these wonderful items and can ensure that the experiences and sacrifices of those connected with the two airfields are remembered and understood by future generations," Thomas Brand, from the firm, said.
In 2024 the Brand family, which owns Grovemere Property, decided to create a new free purpose-built museum following the closure of the RAF Witchford Exhibition, which was located in the foyer of an office building on the business park.
The museum is an unmanned facility with the public gaining entrance via a traffic light system taken from an original Lancaster bomber aircraft [John Devine/BBC]
Brand, a joint managing director of Grovemere Property whose grandfather bought the former RAF Witchford airfield, said the origins of the new museum could be traced to an excavation of a Lancaster bomber crash site at nearby Coveney in 1995.
"The project was supported by Grovemere Property, after local historian Barry Aldridge, who spent decades documenting RAF Witchford's history, got in touch," he said.
Aldridge, who died in 2016, had connections to the airfield that stretched back to childhood, when he explored its derelict buildings.
Artefacts recovered during the Coveney dig included a Lancaster engine, which later became a key exhibit in the previous RAF Witchford Exhibition, and is now the centrepiece at the new museum.
One of the exhibition's photographs shows Princess Elizabeth visiting RAF Witchford in 1944 with King George VI and Queen Elizabeth [RAF Witchford and Mepal Museum]
Brand said that many local people had donated items for the museum, which had given him "goosebump" moments.
"Recently a man gave me an old suitcase which contained his late father's RAF uniform, his medals, flight logs, flying helmet and a personal journal that documented his time in the RAF, it was incredible to see," he said.
RAF Witchford and RAF Mepal played key roles in Bomber Command operations, which saw Lancaster bombers fly missions across occupied Europe [John Devine/BBC]
Brand also said he had witnessed some emotional visitors who had found pictures of their loved ones displayed as part of the exhibit.
He did not disclose how much the museum cost to set-up, but said it was now being run as a charity "to help ensure its long-term future".
The striking design of the building incorporates one side of a Lancaster Bomber fuselage which can be viewed from inside [John Devine/BBC]

articles.title_orig: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
articles.title_zh: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
articles.content_orig:
Prices for gasoline and diesel have more than doubled since the US-Israel conflict with Iran began in February, affecting transport businesses, farmers and anyone who drives a vehicle in America.
Ahead of the critical midterm elections, there have been growing calls for more to be done to reduce the price of fuel, and US President Donald Trump has made several comments and announcements aimed at getting costs down.
The question is: what is he able to do with just a few weeks to go before election day - and will it work?
Trump's announcement of a waiver on the use of red dye diesel at a campaign stop this week underscored the importance of gas prices in a midterm election dominated by affordability issues.
The election comes as there is widespread public concern over the rising costs of fuel, food and other goods. Voters have tied the issue to Trump and his party, weighing down Republicans running in November.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, which has contributed to high diesel and gas prices in the US.
Global oil supplies have been restricted since the conflict in the Middle East effectively halted the usual flow of oil and refined products through the Strait of Hormuz for months.
While the flow of crude oil is nearly back to pre-war levels the price remains above $100 a barrel, and sustained high oil prices have had a knock-on effect for diesel and gasoline.
David Ruisard, pricing manager for commodities intelligence firm Argus says the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine has also impacted oil supplies, contributing to higher fuel prices.
"Our estimates are that your price increase from about $3 a gallon up to $6 a gallon [for diesel] is 60% connected to the Strait of Hormuz, 40% connected to the Russia-Ukraine conflict," he says.
Those higher energy prices are responsible for most of the uptick in inflation this year, Oxford Economics chief US economist Michael Pearce says, which is pushing up interest rates.
"The combined impact of higher rates and higher energy prices is squeezing household budgets and adding to firms' costs," he says.
While prices remain high, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for fuel price tracking website GasBuddy said there have been modest declines recently for both gasoline and diesel.
"A lot of that is likely due to some of the manoeuvres that we've seen the Trump administration employ over the last couple of weeks," he said.
The president announced this week that he would allow so-called red dye diesel - fuel which is used off-road and does not face federal taxes - to be used on US highways without facing federal levies.
Ruisard said the only difference in the diesel used by truck drivers and everyday consumers and the tax-free red dye diesel is the dye itself.
"The problem with that red dye is, it's extremely hard to clean it out of your tank," he explained.
The problem that creates is what happens to trucking companies that use the dyed diesel once the temporary tax relief ends, he said.
"The fines are pretty high for having that in your fuel tank because its considered tax evasion."
The other issue with expanding the use of red dye diesel, according to Ruisard, is that people and businesses - including rail operators - usually set aside a particular amount of the product.
"If suddenly people go out and they start consuming that diesel, that depletes their available supply as well," he said.
But another move from Trump has been more successful, according to analysts.
Last week, the G7 countries announced they would release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to ease supply concerns , following pressure from Trump to do so.
De Haan says the announcement itself – regardless of how much has been released so far – "has worked to push prices down to some degree".
Economist Pearce agreed but warned the release is only a temporary solution.
"As long as energy exports from the Gulf remain disrupted, stocks will need to be drained further to supply the market," he said. "And the need to refill those stocks will mean energy prices remain elevated for a period, even when disruption in the Middle East clears."
Earlier this week, Trump said he was "thinking about" suspending federal tax on gasoline.
De Haan said the president has also been imploring states to cut state taxes on gasoline and several have done so, including Ohio and Georgia.
State taxes form a "moderate portion" of what consumers pay at the pump, and those reductions have helped reduce prices and national averages, he said.
However, suspending or reducing the federal levy on gasoline would require the cooperation of Congress.
"That may be difficult to obtain ahead of the midterm elections," said De Haan.
It is also a costly measure.
De Haan estimated that in Indiana, which cut its tax on gasoline in May, it has cost the state government $1bn (£760m) in lost revenue.
Trump has also previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.
While that would provide partial relief in the Gulf and Midwest, according to Pearce, he adds it would be of "little benefit" to the Northeast and West Coast.
"The policy risks backfiring because it would result in stockpiling of diesel, and as that storage runs out, refineries would need to cut back on production," he said.
"That would raise prices of other energy products, including gasoline."
De Haan believes the president has "basically pulled all of the small levers that a president can pull, and we're still seeing prices very elevated".
"The only way out of this to reduce gas prices in a meaningful way is solve one or both of the geopolitical tensions that are causing high prices," he said.
That means reaching a deal with Iran and helping facilitate an agreement between Ukraine and Russia - which, Pearce said, are issues that cannot be directly controlled by the White House.
Even if those conflicts are resolved, Ruisard said that due to damage to facilities in the Middle East caused by military strikes it would still take production four to six months to return to normal.
"The message to consumers and industry is that regardless of what happens and whether the president is able to successfully negotiate that kind of a deal," he said.
"High prices are here to stay for a little while at least."
Additional reporting from Daniel Bush

articles.title_orig: Zack Polanski’s star is fading
articles.title_zh: Zack Polanski’s star is fading
articles.content_orig:
Sagal Abdi-Wali defeats Green party leader Zack Polanski to retain the Holborn and St Pancras seat for Labour
Report: Labour wins Holborn and St Pancras byelection
Analysis: defeat will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief
Under Green party rules, leaders have to get re-elected every two years, which means there will be a contest next summer. Asked how confident he was of being able to win again, Polanski told Sky News:
double quotation mark What I’m experiencing is the immense amount of people who are saying they’ve never been prouder to be a Green party member.
It is being difficult being leader of any party, particularly the Green party or a decentralised party.
Very often the media – and I think this is fine that they do that - talk about the Green -arty as if we’re like the other parties. But that is a different kind of party. We’re led by the grassroots and ultimately the leader is partly a primary spokesperson for the party. That is difficult. But I signed up for that difficult job, and I’m more than ready to continue.
Asked if he would stand again to be an MP, he replied:
double quotation mark I want to be an MP. I don’t think it’s the be all and end all. I think I’ve demonstrated over the last year that you can create change from outside of parliament.
But, if another seat came up in London where he had a connection, he would stand again, he said.
Compass , the leftwing group campaigning for more pluralism in progressive politics, has issued a long statement saying the Holborn and St Pancras byelection shows why Labour and the Green party should work together.
double quotation mark Last night was both triumph and tragedy for the Green Party. A tragedy because they failed to win a seat that only six months ago they probably would have secured. But weirdly, unexpectedly and unintendedly it is also a triumph. For it is undoubtedly the Greens who have done as much as anyone to rid the country of Starmerism. By mounting a credible political and electoral threat to Labour’s left, realised most spectacularly in the Gorton and Denton by-election and then in May’s local elections, the Greens showed that progressives did have somewhere else to go. And that changed everything. Much to the displeasure of Labour’s right, the party were forced to crown, without a contest, the only politician in the country who has a chance to meet both the twin threats of Reform and the Greens – Andy Burnham …
If we are to rewire the state, bring in proportional representation, tackle the cost of living crisis and even begin to reverse 40 years of neoliberalism, we cannot afford to work against one another.
The Greens are unlikely to replace Labour. But Labour, short on money, short of a mandate and absent of pressure from the Greens, are unlikely to be as radical as the moment demands. We are in this together.
At the Conservative party conference this week, Robert Jenrick , the party’s former justice spokesperson and Kemi Badenoch’s main rival in the leadership contest, was elevated to the status of the party’s chief villain. That’s because of his defection to Reform UK, or his role as a “turncoat” as it was put in the party’s spoof Bayeaux Tapestry.
This morning “the turncoat”, who is now Reform UK’s Treasury spokesperson, gave a speech. It was about the economic choices facing the country, and included criticism of Labour, but Jenrick sounded at his most passionate when he was laying into former colleagues.
Jenrick pointed out that the main policy announcements at the Tory conference favoured the very rich. He explained:
double quotation mark People earning a hundred and fifty grand a year will get free childcare.
People in £2m houses will get a council tax cut.
And if the people who pass away in that mansion have £1m more in the bank, they’ll pay nothing whatsoever.
Kensington Kemi knows who her people are.
Millionaires, not Mansfield.
Jenrick said the main Tory announcement, exempting homes from inheritance tax, would “only benefit one person in 245 in the east Midlands, one in 472 in the north-east [and] almost nobody outside of London and the south-east”.
double quotation mark I’ll just come out and say it.
The party of Disraeli is dead.
He said “The Tory party, unless it is a national party, is nothing.”
Well they’re not even pretending to be a national party now.
What’s left is nothing more than a metropolitan pressure group for the wealthiest.
They have simply given up on the millions of people that have the misfortune of having to work for a living ….
And, who is paying for Badenoch’s bung to Belgravia? Working families.
The Tories decided not to cut the jobs tax [Labour’s rise in employer national insurance], crippling businesses and costing jobs.
She decided not to unfreeze the income tax threshold, which is punishing more and more working people.
She won’t cut taxes on the self-employed. Or make life easier for tradesmen.
In real terms, under her plan, the average worker would pay £265 more than they did under Rachel Reeves.
And she’s taking that 265 quid and giving it to her mates in their central London mansions.
double quotation mark I’ve got to level with you. I have never been happier to be shot of that dying cult.
Because the Tory party has turned its back on everybody I am in politics for.
This wasn’t just a surrender of the red wall. It was the Tories saying to everyone who has to work to get on in life: get stuffed.
Gone are Essex or Workington Man. Gone is Worcester Woman.
In their place, nepo-babies and a new plan to go after Lib Dem voters. Well, fine.
Vivien Lichtenstein , the leader of the Jewish Greens, has called for Zack Polanski to step down as pressure increases on the Green leader to acknowledge anger within the party over a new policy which equates Zionism with racism and calls for the state of Israel to be abolished. Peter Walker has the story.
Here are some more responses to the Holborn and St Pancras byelection result from journalists and commentators.
From Patrick English from YouGov
double quotation mark Just to temper the chat a little bit around what will yes definitely be a morning of disappointment for the Greens... This was not a seat we would *expect* them to win. It is not like other areas in London where they did so well in May (Hackey, Lewisham, Waltham Forest).
From the politics professor Steven Fielding
double quotation mark For any governing party in modern times defending a seat midterm, this is a very good result. But it’s not so good Burnham should even think about holding an early general election.
From the New Statesman’s Ben Walker
double quotation mark Grns performed as Britain Predicts expects. But Lab outperform.
A greater willingness to tactically vote Lab to beat the Grns
A reflection of the Labour bounce in London ...
needs some research. Will change a few dynamics either way.
From Adam Ramsay , a journalist and Green party member
double quotation mark I remember, not so long ago, Greens got c. 4% in a by-election, and my reaction was “well, at least it wasn’t totally humiliating”. The fact that some people think 33% in a longstanding Labour seat in the middle of the Burnham bounce is bad shows how far the party has come.
From the Economist’s Owen Winter
double quotation mark There’s a fine line between righteous anger over the war in Gaza and seeming obsessive/extreme. Big difference speaking to voters in Holborn and St Pancras compared with Gorton and Denton was how many felt the Greens had moved into the second category
From George Eaton from the Arguably Substack
double quotation mark Zack Polanski repeatedly declared that the Greens were “replacing” Labour and said he was “incredibly confident” of winning Holborn & St Pancras. Finishing 12.8 points behind cannot be spun as a “good” result.
Back to the byelection, and the politics professor Rob Ford has written an analysis of the results for Sky News. Here is an excerpt.

articles.title_orig: Mamdani defends Oct. 7 message that angered Jewish leaders, unnerved some Democrats
articles.title_zh: Mamdani defends Oct. 7 message that angered Jewish leaders, unnerved some Democrats
articles.content_orig:
UNION SQUARE, Manhattan (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani defended his Oct. 7 statement on Thursday after facing criticism from some members of the city's Jewish community over remarks that referenced both Israelis killed in the Oct. 7 attacks and Palestinians killed in Gaza.
Mamdani appeared at a news conference in Bushwick on grants to nonprofits Thursday morning, less than 12 hours after demonstrators interrupted a vigil in Union Square for the hundreds of Israelis killed on Oct. 7.
The mayor was escorted past angry pro-Palestinian demonstrators at the vigil as chants echoed through the streets, with some calling him a "traitor."
In a statement issued Wednesday, Mamdani said:
"We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss. The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them - all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes."
Speaking Thursday, Mamdani said he stood by those remarks and rejected suggestions that he should apologize.
"It is critically important to be able to mourn for all of those who were killed—and have been killed since. Especially given that we know this is ongoing, as opposed to something simply that was three years ago," he said.
The mayor's reference to the Israeli military response to Oct. 7 in a statement marking the anniversary drew criticism from some in the city's Jewish community. Mamdani defended his position Thursday.
"We need not choose between which death we will mourn and which we will ignore, that we will reckon with the fact that all of it is to be opposed," he said.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin said she disagreed with the mayor's approach.
"I believe October 7th should focus on the events of October 7th, not on the aftermath, but on the events of October 7th—just as I believe on September 11th, we should focus on the events of September 11th, and that's where I put my focus," she said.
The exchange highlighted differing views among city leaders over how Oct. 7 should be commemorated and discussed.

articles.title_orig: ‘Animals’ Rotten Tomatoes Reviews Bash Ben Affleck Crime Thriller
articles.title_zh: ‘Animals’ Rotten Tomatoes Reviews Bash Ben Affleck Crime Thriller
articles.content_orig:
Things you buy through our links may earn Vox Media a commission.
I like Ben Affleck , I really do. Amid the constant and surely exhausting attention paid to his personal life over the years, the man has carved out an impressive career. As an actor, he probably deserved Oscars (or at least nominations) for The Way Back and The Last Duel . His most recent directorial effort, Air , was one of the best movies of 2023. Before that, The Town and the Best Picture–winning Argo were both solid, and Gone Baby Gone was dazzling. (The less said about Live by Night , however, the better.) And I still think that Best Screenplay Oscar he and Matt Damon won for Good Will Hunting nearly three decades ago was well deserved. I am pro–Ben Affleck. Team Ben. Etc.
So it gives me no pleasure to report that his latest, Animals , which he directed, co-wrote, and stars in (and which is now streaming on Netflix), is a catastrophe. A baffling one to boot. The film is somehow another remake of Akira Kurosawa’s masterpiece High and Low (1963), arriving a little over a year after Spike Lee’s Highest 2 Lowest . (There is no “based on” credit in Animals , however, for either High and Low or King’s Ransom , the 1959 Ed McBain novel that inspired Kurosawa’s picture.) This time, Affleck is the wealthy man at the heart of the mistaken-identity kidnapping thriller. He plays Mark Kimball, an attorney running for mayor of Los Angeles who receives a call saying his young son has been taken and will be released in exchange for $7 million. Unfortunately, Mark has just put every single cent he has into his campaign, so he’s basically broke. With the help of a mysterious, high-powered fixer, Dayle Burton (Gillian Anderson), he finds the money — in exchange, of course, for an extortionate fee. When his son suddenly turns up alive and well, Mark and his psychiatrist wife, Abigail (Kerry Washington), realize that the kidnapper accidentally took the child of Ramón (Luis Gerardo Méndez), their housekeeper’s undocumented day-laborer boyfriend. Are they still willing to pay the ransom now that the kidnapped child is not theirs but that of a poorer family? And what does Dayle (not her real name), who likes to utter aphorisms worthy of a boardroom Sun Tzu (“Leverage is the balance between the allure of incentive and the consequence of refusal”), advise them to do?
Animals wants to be a political and domestic drama as well as a kidnapping thriller, which is certainly not an impossible task when done with a modicum of artistry. The film opens with a campaign commercial for Mark in which he offers bland political bromides against footage of him chatting up ordinary Angelenos. An independent who seems to be running a few points behind in the polls, he thinks winning the Latino vote is the key to victory. His constant drive to succeed appears to have alienated Abigail, to the extent that she’s currently having an affair with Ron (Ray Fisher), a teacher who’s just left his family and expects her to do the same (on the eve of her husband’s election campaign, no less, which definitely marks Ron as a smart, un-insane guy). The script tries to weave together these elements. Mark’s ambition, entitlement, and do-gooding hypocrisy have clearly undercut his family’s needs, and now, this high-pressure situation is exposing all these simmering domestic conflicts.
But the writing is ghastly. Most of the time, Mark just flails, complains, and pouts like a giant baby, and Affleck’s twitchy, rapid-fire delivery can’t give the character any life or depth. There’s emotion in his performance, but it rarely feels like the right emotion. He looks and sounds like an angry actor trying to get through a scene instead of a man in the middle of an impossible dilemma. Maybe that’s the point — the film seeks to interrogate Mark’s narcissism — but every interaction feels like it’s been flattened into a series of predictable accusations instead of something that might provoke surprise or reflection. One climactic, teary confrontation between Mark and his wife, which perhaps could have been the film’s emotional high point, rings so false I inadvertently started laughing out loud.
And at the risk of making a “The food is terrible … and such small portions” criticism, I’ll add that nothing feels fleshed out either. Abigail’s affair is briefly touched on and ultimately abandoned. (Did poor Ray Fisher get his scenes cut again ??) Anderson seems to have a good time as the domineering, white-pantsuited and English-accented Dayle, all attitude and posture, but she also seems to be in a different movie. In fact, it is entirely possible that she’s in the movie Animals should have been, an over-the-top and self-aware kidnapping thriller instead of a failed exploration of race, power, and money. The film does give Ramón, the undocumented father of the actual kidnapped child, more to do than previous versions, as he starts trying to take the law into his own hands; that might have made for an interesting story thread (and a refreshing twist on the original), but here it feels tacked on. In the meantime, as Mark’s campaign manager, Sam, Steven Yeun serves mostly to push and prod his boss into making risky decisions, but one does wonder why such a talented actor has been cast in a one-note part. What is anybody doing here? What on earth happened to this movie?
Animals begins awkwardly, proceeds chaotically, and ends ludicrously, in a way that suggests that either a more considered ending was abandoned along the way or that Affleck wanted to distinguish his variation on High and Low by doing away with any of the things that made the story’s previous iterations interesting. I’ve never read the McBain novel, but Kurosawa’s and Lee’s films are both steeped in class and economic milieus: They’re structured around forcing their protagonists to break out of their isolation and confront their privilege, with the kidnapper becoming something of a mirror image of the ostensible hero; Kurosawa’s ends with a literal mirror image. Affleck’s instead ends with one of the dumbest and most predictably action-y finales of recent years, so much so that it made me wonder if it was trying to be a parody. There are enough seemingly unintentional laughs here that … maybe it is? Perhaps the actor-director is trying to borrow a page from his bitterly funny David Fincher hit, Gone Girl (another kidnapping thriller, sort of), but Animals has none of that earlier picture’s wit or Grand Guignol extremes or gonzo structure.
Each adaptation should stand on its own, of course, and Kurosawa films have proven quite malleable over the years. ( Yojimbo , itself inspired by Dashiell Hammett’s Red Harvest , became A Fistful of Dollars and Last Man Standing ; Seven Samurai became The Magnificent Seven and Battle Beyond the Stars and A Bug’s Life and Rebel Moon and The Magnificent Seven again; Rashomon became The Outrage and an episode of Frasier ; hell, even Ikiru became Living ; oh, and The Hidden Fortress became Star Wars .) That malleability is the adapter’s friend. The stories have strong armature, so just about all other details and threads can be changed. A High and Low set in the world of a high-stakes campaign isn’t a terrible idea, potentially unraveling the entitlement, ego, and isolation of the political class. And Los Angeles, with its many simmering social conflicts and resentments, is an ideal setting for something like this. All of which makes Animals ’s failure that much more heartbreaking and enraging. Oh, well. At least we’ll always have Air .

Beijing could leverage the yuan’s low interest rate to increase the currency’s worldwide use, an expert says
The 10-year US Treasury yield was 5.22 per cent on Thursday, compared with 1.69 per cent for Chinese government bonds on their first trading day after the National Day holiday – a gap of about 3.5 percentage points, compared with a record 3.7 percentage points on September 9.
Jiang Zhenlong, an associate research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Finance and Banking, argued that higher US yields weaken the appeal of yuan assets and add pressure on the exchange rate and capital flows, but also raise dollar funding costs.

articles.title_orig: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.title_zh: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.content_orig:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaii News Now interviewed U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda and state Sen. Brenton Awa, candidates for Hawaii’s 2nd Congressional District, about the Iran war, aid to Israel and immigration enforcement.
Awa said he is seeking only one term in Congress.
“I only want to go for two years, one term, and the reason is, is because I don’t care about all of those world policies and all the votes that’ll have to be taken. I’ll have to care when I am taking it,” Awa said.
Awa said he wants money spent on the Iran war and support for Israel to instead go to American families dealing with disaster.
“But my biggest focus, if we’re going to send billions of dollars to Israel or another country, my only concern is why isn’t that money coming to Hawaii,” Awa said.
Tokuda said ending the war is the best way to reduce energy costs. She opposes aid to Israel because of its treatment of Palestinians.
“It’s a genocide,” Tokuda said.
“When you take a look at the weapons they are using, it was our weapons, which is why I voted against funding weapons sales to Israel for now, because that is blood on our hands,” Tokuda said.
On immigration enforcement, Awa does not oppose mass deportation but said he believes ICE has been too violent.
“The idea is good. The way they go and carry it out, and I don’t know,” Awa said. “I’m not there on the ground, so I don’t know, but other than what I see, through you guys, the media. But when you see people dying, there is no way that that should ever happen.”
Tokuda said there will be pressure to fix immigration laws after the election.
“We absolutely have to pass some kind of meaningful bipartisan immigration reform that protects our borders, that creates legal pathways to citizenship and doesn’t result in Americans getting executed in our streets,” Tokuda said.
Awa acknowledges the odds are stacked against him in a district that has never elected a Republican, and GOP voters have been discouraged by President Trump’s unpopularity.
Awa did not have to give up his Senate seat to run for Congress and has two years remaining on his term.

articles.title_orig: The advice immigration attorneys have for Microsoft workers worried about their green cards
articles.title_zh: The advice immigration attorneys have for Microsoft workers worried about their green cards
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration's Thursday declaration that it was suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal visa sponsorship program is reverberating through the tech industry.
Immigration attorneys told Business Insider that employees on H-1B visas working at Microsoft, Adobe, and the other named tech companies should seek counsel and get clarity about their status in light of the suspensions.
Individual cases may vary, and the attorneys spoke in general terms about the advice they would give without knowing a client's specific circumstances or status.
"This is a time where immigrants, high-skilled immigrants, really need to pay attention to laws," said Tahmina Watson, a business immigration attorney at Watson Immigration Law in Seattle. "Things are changing on a dime," she added.
Business Insider spoke to eight immigration attorneys on Thursday in the wake of the announcement, as part of our ongoing series, " H-1B Fallout: 1 Year Later ," which explores how foreign workers are navigating a rapidly changing US immigration landscape.
Some of the immigration attorneys said the suspensions were likely to be challenged in court. Others said they were the latest in a series of US measures targeting foreign workers. One attorney suggested they would only impact a relatively small group of workers.
"Most people will either be able to wait it out or have time to switch jobs," said Loren Locke, an attorney at Locke Immigration Law in Atlanta.
The Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program is an initial step that employers generally must complete before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based visa, requiring them to show that no qualified and available US workers could fill the role.
Vice President JD Vance said at a press conference on Thursday that Microsoft had "abused" this system by laying off American workers and using it to hire foreign ones, who he said were paid less. "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
A Microsoft spokesperson pointed Business Insider to a blog post the company published Thursday, which said "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company said it pays its H-1B employees "the same as any other employees doing comparable work."
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said at the press conference that the government would not accept any new PERM applications or process any pending ones for the named companies, which, in addition to Microsoft and Adobe, also include tech outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini.
In suspending new and pending PERM applications, the Trump administration left a very specific group of H-1B visa holders in limbo, said Matthew Maiona, an immigration attorney at Maiona Ward in Boston.
Maiona said that a hypothetical employee at Microsoft or Adobe, six years into an H-1B visa, could now, in theory, be ordered to appear in immigration court under this new suspension.
"You could be in trouble if you cannot qualify for another non-immigrant visa classification," Maiona said. "You may have to leave the United States."
But Locke said workers would only face potential removal if they exhausted their H-1B eligibility and could not secure an extension or another legal basis — of which there are several — to remain in the country.
Though H-1B visas have a statutory maximum of six years before expiring, they can be extended past that number if workers have made sufficient progress toward obtaining a green card, she said.
"If the goal is to crush H-1B workers, it's not great, but it's not really crushing them either," Locke said.
Todd Pomerleau, an immigration attorney based in Boston, said that with uncertainty around the extent and enforcement of the suspensions, "anybody who's concerned about their immigration status needs to seek competent counsel."
Some immigration attorneys who spoke with Business Insider said they expected the Trump administration's move to be challenged in a lawsuit that would argue the suspensions are outside the Labor Department's legal authority.
"I assume, by next week, we will start seeing lawsuits," said Kripa Upadhyay, the co-chair of Buchalter's Immigration & Global Mobility Practice, a Seattle firm.
Ted Chiappari, the head of immigration law at Duane Morris LLP, said federal statute only allows the Department of Labor to unilaterally suspend an employer from using the PERM program for 180 days.
"That gives the employer notice that there's an investigation going on, and at the end of that investigation, if they find something inappropriate, they have six years to decide whether to debar an employer," he said.
And even then, Chiappari said, they can only debar an employer for up to three years.
Few attorneys interviewed by Business Insider said they were surprised by the measure. Mostly, they saw it as another salvo in what they described as the Trump administration's ongoing crackdown on foreign workers.
Upadhyay said that just the day before, she had spoken with a Microsoft employee on an H-1B whose spouse also was on an H-1B.
The person's H-1B extension was running out, and they now faced the "impossible decision" of moving to their home country, leaving behind their spouse and two US citizen children.
"I have children to support," Upadhyay recalled the worker saying. "What happens now?"
Upadhyay expects to get more of these calls.

articles.title_orig: Princeton Celebrates Anne Carson, a Nobel Prize Winner Who Was Denied Tenure
articles.title_zh: Princeton Celebrates Anne Carson, a Nobel Prize Winner Who Was Denied Tenure
articles.content_orig:
Anne Carson, the Canadian writer and classicist whose work blends verse, prose and essay with influences from classical myths, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature for her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”
Carson, 76, is an accomplished classicist who has taught at multiple colleges in the US and Canada while also producing works like “The Beauty of the Husband,” “An Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse,” and “Nox.” Her distinctive essays, prose and poetry, in which the ancient and modern live side-by-side, have garnered her critical acclaim.
Carson’s “playful dialogue with the classical tradition has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Nobel committee said in a statement.
The prize, announced at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm on Thursday, carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million).
Carson is widely known for hybrid style where she balances multiple ideas, genres and forms. “Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chairman of the Nobel Committee for Literature.
For example, in “Autobiography of Red,” the work that made her name, her long narrative verse is framed by an erudite, enigmatic discussion of Stesichorus, the Greek poet who inspired her. In Stesichorus’ original myth, Heracles – better known by his Latin name of Hercules – kills the winged monster Geryon and steals his red cattle as one of his 12 labors. In Carson’s 1998 retelling, she recasts Geryon as a “tender ‘hero’ devoted to his mother,” who “having earlier been subjected to sexual assaults at the hands of his brother, falls in love with the smug and boorish Heracles,” the Nobel committee said.
Such a complicated form belies the simplicity of much of the language in it. “Somehow Geryon made it to adolescence.// Then he met Herakles and the kingdoms of his life all shifted down a few notches,” Carson writes. “They were two superior eels//at the bottom of the tank and they recognized each other like italics.”
Carson was in Iceland, “listening to the wind,” when she discovered she had won the Nobel Prize, according to Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy.
“She was taken by surprise but very happy – I could hear that in her voice,” Carlberg said.
Much of Carson’s early career was dominated by her work in classics – she studied for her bachelor’s, master’s and doctorate degrees at the University of Toronto and also received a diploma in classics from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Although she published an essay and her Ph.D. thesis in her thirties, it wasn’t until she was 42 years old that her first book of poems “Short Talks” was published. Three more works followed before “Autobiography of Red” marked her out as a critical favorite.
“The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos,” which charts the breakdown of a marriage between two unnamed characters, came three years later. For that work, Carson became the first female winner of the prestigious T.S. Eliot Prize in 2001. She is the 19th woman of the 122 individuals who have won the Nobel Prize for literature.
Nobel Prize in medicine awarded to trio for technique that helps decode mysteries of the brain
Carson is notoriously private about her personal life, but her 2010 work “Nox” reflects on the life and death of her estranged brother, Michael. It is not a traditional book, as such, but a “box containing an accordion-fold-out of picture, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother,” Olsson said.
Carson has also produced several translations of classical texts and ventured into other artforms, collaborating with visual artists, choreographers, opera and theater directors. The transition into various other artistic fields “demonstrates the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems, which in turn lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene,” Olsson added.
Last year, the prize went to László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art,” the committee said.
In 2024, South Korean author Han Kang was honored by the committee for her “intense poetic prose that confronts historical traumas and exposes the fragility of human life.”
Literature is the fourth prize to be handed out this week, after achievements in medicine, physics and chemistry. The Nobel Peace Prize is set to be revealed on Friday, followed by the winners in economics on October 12.

articles.title_orig: Apple rolls out AT&T carrier update for iPhone 18 Pro Max on iOS 27.2 beta
articles.title_zh: Apple rolls out AT&T carrier update for iPhone 18 Pro Max on iOS 27.2 beta
articles.content_orig:
After releasing a carrier settings update last week to address cellular issues affecting some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, Apple is now rolling out a different carrier bundle update for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta. Here are the details.
Last Friday, Apple confirmed to 9to5Mac that a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T were experiencing an issue that could cause their devices to lose cellular service and become unable to make calls.
Apple said iOS 27.0.1 , alongside a new carrier settings update, was meant to prevent the issue from affecting additional devices. However, iPhones that had already lost service would still require a hardware replacement.
Tonight, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple began rolling out another carrier bundle update for iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, this time specifically for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta.
Apple has just released an emergency carrier bundle update for AT&T users using an iPhone 18 Pro Max on 27.2 beta. Version 72.0.3 up from 72.0.2 This comes after Apple released 72.1 for iOS 27.0 users last week
Reports of the problem first surfaced in late September, when some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T found that their devices had suddenly lost access to calls, texts, and cellular data, instead displaying “SOS” in the status bar.
Notably, the issue has only affected the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which uses a Qualcomm modem in the United States. The iPhone 18 Pro, which uses Apple’s C2 modem, has not been affected.
Apple’s carrier settings update released last week brought AT&T users on iOS 27.0 to version 72.1. However, users running the iOS 27.2 beta remained on the older 72.0.2 carrier bundle.
Tonight’s release reportedly bumps those devices to carrier bundle version 72.0.3, likely extending Apple’s AT&T carrier changes to iPhone 18 Pro Max users who are testing the iOS 27.2 beta.

articles.title_zh: American Oil Refiners Are Printing Money as Wars Shrink Global Energy Supplies
articles.content_orig:
Global refined product supply continues to tighten, pushing U.S. independent refiners toward an unprecedented earnings peak. Damage to Middle East refineries from the war, Ukraine's sustained strikes on Russian refining facilities, and reduced fuel exports from Asian countries have driven diesel and gasoline prices up far more than crude oil, positioning Valero Energy (VLO), Marathon Petroleum (MPC), and Phillips 66 (PSX) to post third-quarter earnings that could surpass their second-quarter highs across the board, with some metrics set to shatter all-time records.
According to Wall Street analyst forecasts cited by The Wall Street Journal, the three companies will report results between late October and early November. JPMorgan estimates that Valero's U.S. Gulf Coast refineries achieved an average spread of $47.11 per barrel between crude purchase prices and refined product selling prices in Q3, far above the $30.28 recorded in Q2. At that level, Valero's Q3 pre-tax profit could reach $8.95 billion, up 50% quarter-over-quarter and 24% above the quarterly record set in mid-2022.
Piper Sandler projects Marathon Petroleum's Q3 earnings per share could exceed seven times the year-ago figure; Phillips 66's refining segment profit is also expected to surpass its previous record.
Crack spreads drive profit surge
The core driver of this earnings expansion is the refining industry's key metric—the "crack spread"—the difference between crude oil purchase costs and selling prices of refined products such as diesel and gasoline. While crude prices rose in Q3, refined product prices surged even more sharply, rapidly widening the profit refiners earn per barrel processed.
The average U.S. retail diesel price recently spiked to a record $6.53 per gallon. While it has since pulled back, it remains at extremely elevated levels. South Korea's iM Securities estimates that damaged refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East alone accounts for more than 6% of total global capacity; since February, diesel export disruptions from the two regions have totaled approximately 1.6 million barrels per day.
Note: Forecasts from JPMorgan and Piper Sandler
Supply gap continues to widen
The current global refining system faces not a crude oil shortage, but a severe shortfall in processing capacity. Industrial Info Resources data shows approximately 12.1% of global refining capacity was offline as of September. Goldman Sachs estimates roughly 2 million barrels per day of refining capacity in the Middle East remains unable to operate normally.
Crude oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered significantly from the early stages of the war, but supplies of refined products—diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel—are recovering far more slowly than crude. The market is gradually resolving the question of "is there enough crude," but has yet to solve the problem of "are there enough refineries to turn crude into fuel."
The Russia-Ukraine conflict has further widened this gap. JPMorgan tallies that Ukraine has struck approximately 15 Russian refining facilities since late July, knocking close to 2 million barrels per day of refining capacity out of the market. Goldman Sachs expects that even if Brent crude falls back to around $80 per barrel, the diesel squeeze may not disappear in tandem. The bank forecasts that global diesel and jet fuel crack spreads could still average above $40 per barrel in 2027—more than double the typical level of around $20.
Dramatic re-rating of stock prices and market value
Earnings expectations are already fully reflected in the stock market. Valero, Marathon, and Phillips 66 all hit record highs on Thursday, with year-to-date gains exceeding 100% each and a combined market value increase of approximately $224 billion. Over the same period, the S&P 500 rose only about 13%. Valero's stock closed at $413 on September 18, up roughly 144% year-to-date.
Wall Street views on the outlook are diverging. UBS raised its Valero price target from $355 to $450, maintaining a "Buy" rating; Piper Sandler lifted its target from $329 to $435; Raymond James also raised its target from $350 to $450 in September. These firms broadly expect the diesel supply shortage to persist into next year, and have accordingly raised their 2027 crack spread forecasts by roughly $5 per barrel, while setting refining EBITDA expectations at 1.36 times the Wall Street average.
Morgan Stanley, while sharply raising its Valero target from $255 to $411, maintained a "Neutral" rating, arguing the current stock price already reflects much of the industry's improved fundamentals.
Why new capacity investment is absent
Such high profits have not prompted U.S. refiners to build new capacity at scale. A major refinery project requires billions of dollars in investment, and typically takes years from planning and permitting to full operation—and companies are not confident that the current high-margin environment created by war and supply disruptions will persist until a new project comes online.
U.S. refining capacity has generally declined over the past decade. Data shows U.S. refining capacity peaked at approximately 18.6 million barrels per day in 2017, fell to 17.6 million barrels per day by 2025, and is expected to decline further to roughly 17.45 million barrels per day this year.
The U.S. government has recently convened refiners to discuss expanding domestic refining capacity. The Trump administration and industry figures have also discussed restarting two recently closed California refineries—Phillips 66's Los Angeles-area facility and Valero's Benicia refinery. The two facilities previously accounted for roughly 20% of California's refining capacity combined. But restarting them also faces equipment, logistics, and crude supply challenges; even if companies decide to resume production, it could take months.
John Auers, refined products analyst at Novi Labs, believes global refining capacity is currently "extremely tight," and U.S. refiners could maintain elevated profitability through 2027, but companies are still unlikely to launch major new construction projects because the industry broadly views the current environment as abnormal.
Valero's competitive advantage also extends to crude procurement costs. More than 60% of the company's U.S. refining capacity is concentrated on the Gulf Coast, compared with 42% for Marathon Petroleum and 27% for Phillips 66. The Gulf Coast is the hub of major U.S. pipelines and import/export terminals, offering relatively convenient access to crude from the U.S., Canada, Venezuela, and Central and South America. iM Securities analysis notes that in Q1, Valero increased its use of Canadian crude—up to $26 per barrel cheaper than WTI—and resumed Venezuelan crude imports, with this procurement optimization contributing roughly 30% of the refining segment's incremental profit for the quarter.
Valero returned $2.6 billion to shareholders in Q2, equivalent to 59% of adjusted operating cash flow. As of end-June, the company held $7.9 billion in cash and cash equivalents, above the $4 billion to $5 billion range it considers appropriate. The company has not cut its dividend since 2012 and has consistently repurchased shares, with shares outstanding last year down 27% from 2021. Its medium-to-long-term policy is to return more than 50% of EBITDA to shareholders.
Market participants caution that the current high-margin environment carries multiple risk variables. Hurricanes could force Gulf Coast refinery shutdowns, and changes in Venezuelan crude policy could affect feedstock supply. Once crack spreads normalize, refining earnings will inevitably retreat from their current abnormally elevated levels.
