articles.title_orig: Florida officials urge preparation as state braces for first hurricane in two years
articles.title_zh: Florida officials urge preparation as state braces for first hurricane in two years
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias is headed for a Gulf Coast landfall Friday night with life-threatening storm surge, rainfall flooding and high winds. It will then spread its heavy rain and wind inland over the Southeast this weekend.
Preparations to protect life and property from damaging winds and storm surge near the northern Gulf Coast should be finished by tonight.
New this morning: Isaias continues to strengthen and should become a Category 3 major hurricane later this morning.
(MORE: Hurricane Isaias maps tracker | Live updates )
Isaias is centered in the Gulf about 200 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River. The storm is moving to the north-northeast at 15 mph.
It's expected to strengthen more this morning and then will take a more northerly track to landfall.
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
Storm surge warning : Mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwannee River, Florida. A storm surge watch extends south to Yankeetown, Florida.
Hurricane warning: Along the Gulf Coast from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida, and also inland in parts of southwest Alabama and the western Florida Panhandle (shaded in purple on the map below).
(MORE: What you can do today to prepare for Isaias )
Tropical storm warning : Along the Gulf Coast from the Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line south of New Orleans to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and east of the Bay/Gulf County line to the Aucilla River, Florida. These warnings also extend to much of inland southern Alabama, parts of southeast Mississippi, the rest of the Florida Panhandle not in hurricane alerts and extreme southwestern Georgia (shaded in red in the map below).
Tropical storm watch: From parts of eastern Mississippi, extending north into central Alabama and parts of western Georgia (shaded in yellow in the map below).
( MORE: What all these tropical terms mean )
Isaias is benefiting from Gulf water temperatures well into the 80s and a moist air mass, both favorable for intensification until early Friday. Additionally, Isaias will pass over some of the warmest waters of the Gulf for several hours during the time of the day more favorable for development. This could boost Isaias to Category 3 status by later this morning.
To be clear: We are not expecting Isaias to make landfall as a major hurricane.
Isaias will experience increasing wind shear as it moves farther north Friday nearing its Gulf Coast landfall.
Wind shear is hostile for both developing tropical systems and hurricanes. You can see the wind shear map below; the colors in darker purple and white indicate strong wind shear.
Therefore, Isaias is likely to lose some wind intensity closer to landfall.
For now, the most likely intensity near landfall is a Category 1 or a Category 2 hurricane. But a slight drop in wind speeds right before landfall will do little to diminish the storm's impacts.
(MORE: What you need to know during hurricane season )
The most significant impacts will be felt along and to the east of the storm's track and its inland remnant.
Isaias is also expected to grow in size near landfall, expanding its footprint of impacts.
The map below shows how much inundation of normally dry ground may occur near the coast from water pushing in from the Gulf as the center of Isaias moves ashore Friday night into early Saturday morning, according to the National Hurricane Center.
These values represent the peak flood levels if the storm surge happens around high tide.
This is a life-threatening storm surge, especially in areas shaded in yellow and orange in the map below.
Damaging winds are most likely in areas covered by hurricane and tropical storm alerts, shown in the graphic near the top of this article, from extreme southeast Louisiana and southeastern Mississippi to central and southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and parts of western Georgia.
Winds of at least 40 mph could arrive as soon as this afternoon and continue at least through Saturday morning near the Gulf Coast.
High winds are also possible Saturday into at least Sunday morning farther inland in the Tennessee Valley and Smoky Mountains.
Downed trees, power lines and power outages that could last for hours or multiple days are possible in these areas. Trees could be toppled easier in ground soaked by heavy rain.
Heavy rain from Isaias will arrive along the Gulf Coast Friday, then will push far inland through the rest of the weekend.
As much as 15 inches of rain could fall locally near the Gulf Coast, especially east of the track of the center where training heavy rainbands may persist the longest. Most other areas near the Gulf Coast are forecast to pick up 4 to 8 inches of rain.
Most of the rest of the Southeast is forecast to pick up 1 to 5 inches of rain.
Locally flash flooding is possible over most of the Southeast, Appalachians and parts of the Ohio Valley and mid-Atlantic this weekend.
(MORE: What is the 'dirty side' of a hurricane? )
As often is the case with landfalling hurricanes, there is a threat for tornadoes in outer rainbands as the center approaches land Friday, then possibly again Saturday in parts of the Southeast.
Today, conditions will begin to deteriorate along the Gulf Coast.
Anywhere from New Orleans to Tallahassee should see the worst of the rain and winds, but rainfall is also expected in central Florida and even into southeastern Georgia.
Saturday, Isaias will move farther inland and weaken, but its impacts will be far from over.
Heavy rainfall and powerful winds will spread inland across the Southeast. Cities like Jackson, Memphis, Nashville, Atlanta, Wilmington, Charleston, Tallahassee and Orlando could see the worst of the conditions.
Sunday, what is left of Isaias will continue to move north, bringing rainfall to parts of the Great Lakes, mid-Atlantic and even the Northeast.
Rainfall will still be ongoing as far south as Savannah and Nashville but will spread to Charlotte, Virginia Beach, Washington, New York City, Philadelphia and Baltimore. Rain could even fall for Cincinnati and Detroit.
If you're near the Gulf Coast in areas covered by hurricane warnings and/or storm surge warnings, complete your preparations now.
If asked to evacuate by local officials, please consider doing so for your own safety.
If remaining home, be prepared for power outages that could last at least several hours or possibly multiple days.
Avoid flood-prone areas and never drive into flooded stretches of roads.
Impact risk The map below shows the general risk from Isaias and its inland remnant, including from rainfall flooding, winds and storm surge near the coast. This map will update throughout the duration of the storm.
The impact levels on the map mean:
(MORE: Stay prepared this hurricane season )
Isaias ( ees-ah-EE-ahs) is one of the trickier names to pronounce on this year's list. To hear the correct pronunciation, listen here .
Isaias replaced "Ike" on one of the Atlantic name lists after that name was retired following the destructive, deadly 2008 hurricane .
It wasn't used during its first year of eligibility in 2014, since we only reached the eighth name, Hanna, that year.
However, the name was used in 2020 for a storm that eventually tracked up the East Coast with destructive winds.

articles.title_orig: European industry groups call for urgent EU action on China trade
articles.title_zh: European industry groups call for urgent EU action on China trade
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS, Oct 8 (Reuters) – Forty-four European industry associations urged EU members on Thursday to take immediate action to combat ​what they said were unfair Chinese ‌trade practices threatening EU manufacturing and risking further job losses.
The call from the associations representing sectors including metals, chemicals and automotive parts comes a ‌week ​before EU leaders convene ⁠in Brussels to ⁠discuss how best to tackle a growing trade deficit with China of more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion) a day.
The associations said ​the European Union should more effectively use all instruments available to impose trade ⁠defence measures and ⁠adopt a broader approach to look ​at entire value chains, while avoiding negative ​impacts on close European partners, such as ‌Britain, Norway and Switzerland.
They said the European Commission needed more staff to process complaints more rapidly. They also called for ⁠new tools to deal with state-driven distortions.
EU leaders at the summit are set to discuss Franco-German ⁠proposals for ‌expanded trade defence published ⁠on Monday and European Trade Commissioner Maros ​Sefcovic’s ‌two-day trip to Beijing ending ​on Friday. ⁠Sefcovic is seeking to persuade China to agree to cut exports to the EU in one sector, most likely hybrid vehicles.
(Reporting by Philip Blenkinsop; Editing by ​Cynthia Osterman)

articles.title_zh: Exclusive: House Democrats ask Kimberly Guilfoyle for records related to alleged pay-to-play scheme
articles.content_orig:
Kimberly Guilfoyle faces renewed scrutiny over her conduct as U.S. ambassador to Greece after a Donald Trump donor alleged she offered him access to administration officials in exchange for paying a $100,000 American Express bill. The allegation has prompted calls for an investigation, while her lawyer disputes the messages behind the claim.
Eric Deters, a lawyer and former congressional candidate, made the accusation during a Thursday interview with MS NOW. He said Guilfoyle approached him last year, before her Senate confirmation hearing, and offered him connections to government officials if he covered the outstanding balance. Deters called the arrangement "absolutely" a quid pro quo and said he never owed her money. Deters also called Guilfoyle a "grifter."
Messages Deters shared with The Wall Street Journal reportedly show Guilfoyle promising he would be her "Trump ride or die" if he arranged the payment. In another exchange, she allegedly urged him to stop "papering" their conversations and use Signal instead, warning that written records could jeopardize her ambassadorship.
Jesse Binnall, Guilfoyle's attorney, challenged the messages' authenticity in comments to the Journal. He also maintained that Guilfoyle was owed money for travel and speaking engagements she completed before her nomination. Deters rejected that explanation, saying he did not owe her a balance (via The Guardian ).
Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to address the latest allegations when reporters questioned him in Athens on Wednesday and Thursday. He nevertheless called Guilfoyle "a strong ambassador." Vice President JD Vance also expressed reservations about the alleged arrangement but said he "doesn't know the full details."
The dispute follows earlier reporting by The Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle invited Greek lobbyists to official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of a Greek construction and energy company. Those allegations had already drawn concern from Democratic lawmakers overseeing foreign affairs.

articles.title_orig: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
articles.title_zh: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.
Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.
Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable companies in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."
Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.
"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.
The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.
Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.
The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.
The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped at 85,000 per year.
A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.
Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.
The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.
She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.
According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.
"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.
Satya Nadella, Microsoft's long-time chief executive, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.
Introducing Nadella during the event, Trump said the White House was "honoured" to be awarding the medal to him and that it was "so well-deserved".
Other tech industry figures to receive medals from Trump were Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Michael Dell.
Nadella and most of the other medal recipients were also present at other recent White House events, including a lunch on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.
Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.
"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.
Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating that grace period altogether.
Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.
None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.
The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.
The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.
During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

articles.title_orig: Two men arrested after breaking into UK airbase used by US, counterterrorism police say
articles.title_zh: Two men arrested after breaking into UK airbase used by US, counterterrorism police say
articles.content_orig:
British counterterrorism police are investigating after two Latvian men were arrested inside a Royal Air Force base used by US personnel, authorities said on Thursday.
The arrests come weeks after a suspected plot targeting another British airbase used by the US military raised concerns about security at military sites across Britain.
Police said there was nothing so far to suggest the incident at RAF Molesworth in eastern England was linked to the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by the US military to launch missions against Iran.
The men were discovered after Ministry of Defence Police found an abandoned vehicle during a security patrol at RAF Molesworth, about 100 km (60 miles) north of London, and raised the alarm.
Subsequent checks uncovered a small breach in the perimeter fence and the two men, aged 32 and 36, were arrested inside the base.
They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage, before being re-arrested on suspicion of “entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK” under the National Security Act 2023.
RAF Molesworth is used by US personnel and hosts intelligence analysis and command operations, as well as a NATO intelligence centre. It is not used for flying operations.
Last month, several men were arrested over a suspected plot to attack RAF Fairford, 90 miles (145 km) ‌west of London. The British government has linked the suspected plot to Iran , which denied any involvement.
The incident raised concerns over security at Britain’s military bases, particularly those used by US forces. The US said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of its bombers from Fairford.
“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week,” Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said in a statement.
Police said both men were resident in Britain and that officers were searching two addresses in the area around Peterborough, a nearby city.
Bomb disposal officers checked the abandoned vehicle but found nothing of concern, police said.
“We are highly vigilant about potential threats to our military sites and work closely with the police to keep them secure,” defense minister Wes Streeting said in a post on X.
A US Air Force spokesperson said they appreciated the swift response and support from local law enforcement.
“We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities,” the spokesperson added.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon unveils US$350 million quantum computing push as China rivalry grows
articles.title_zh: Pentagon unveils US$350 million quantum computing push as China rivalry grows
articles.content_orig:
New initiative aims to strengthen US military capabilities as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in advanced technology
The Pentagon announced on Thursday a new multimillion-dollar initiative for “maintaining American leadership” in quantum computing capabilities amid accelerating competition between the US and China over the military application of advanced technology.
In a press release, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defence for Research and Engineering, which serves as the US Department of Defence’s chief technology adviser, announced that the new initiative, worth around US$350 million, is aimed at strengthening US leadership in quantum computing capabilities to “support national security”.
Quantum computing dominance is a “critical priority” for the Trump administration, said Emil Michael, undersecretary of defence for research and engineering, citing a June executive order to accelerate the technology’s deployment, commercialisation and domestic manufacturing across the US.
“Maintaining American leadership in this field is essential to preserving our technological edge,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
articles.title_zh: Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
articles.content_orig:
MADRID — María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis , died on Wednesday while hospitalized.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the way on social media offering his condolences after housing activists and Abascal’s lawyer announced her death. Known widely as “Maricarmen,” she had become a symbol for renters struggling with Spain’s housing affordability crisis.
“All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Sánchez said in a post on X. “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace.”
Elderly Madrid resident who was forcibly evicted dies at 87
The emotions ran into anger on the street among the protesters gathered near Spain’s Parliament who chanted, “Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!”
Iciar López, a 32-year-old psychologist, shared her feelings with The Associated Press at the protest in Madrid.
“A great deal of sorrow. And above all, the thought that she is the cause, the head of this whole revolution that has happened, and that she can’t see it,” she said. “It makes me very sad that she can’t see if anything comes of it, if there is any result from all that she has fought for, as well. That’s what angers me the most, honestly.”
Spaniards increasingly frustrated by housing costs periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers. But a fresh wave of indignation has swept Spain since Sept. 23, when Maricarmen, who used a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her home of seven decades after police cordoned off the street and removed protesters. She was taken to a hospital because of her fragile health.
Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country.
Maricarmen’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, did not disclose the cause of death when she confirmed it to Cadena Ser radio. Duro said that she and the activists were all devastated.
“Maricarmen’s case, which captured media attention and traveled around the world, leaves us the image of the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the impact they can have on people’s health,” Duro said.
She had been expected to return home after leaving the hospital. The real estate company that evicted her in order to rent the property at a much higher price eventually caved in under immense public pressure and agreed to let her return to the apartment.
“Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return home, this solution came too late,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said in a statement Wednesday. “It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal.”
The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, according to the real estate website Idealista. Spain’s government said that 26% of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the European Union average of 18% of renters who do so.
Protesters camped in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square held a minute of silence after learning of her death.
Maricarmen spent almost her entire life in her apartment, where she first lived with her parents and brother. She later worked as a secretary for the board of a pharmaceutical company, Spanish daily El País reported. She said both her parents died in the apartment.
After retiring in 1998, she spent her days walking around the neighborhood, doing errands and taking care of the precious items in her home. The paper reported that black-and-white family photographs were among the only things she had brought with her to the hospital.
“Maricarmen only wanted to die in her home. She wasn’t asking for anything else,” Eugenio Melchor, 22, said at the protest in Madrid. “She was dying in her home and she almost did. They have killed her. I mean, there’s no other word for it, and I hope those responsible for this pay and go to trial.”
Maricarmen’s plight galvanized a social movement, prompted Spain’s unions to announce a general strike next month and intensified pressure on political leaders. Sánchez called an early election Monday after his government failed last week to push emergency housing measures through Parliament. He now hopes the issue will reinvigorate his Socialist Party and help him form a new government after the Nov. 29 election.
Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez also expressed condolences, writing on X: “I deeply lament the death of Maricarmen. My condolences to those who accompanied her and fought by her side until the end.”
Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who hopes to unseat Sánchez and his left-wing coalition, also offered condolences.
“I want to express my condolences to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage,” the Popular Party leader wrote. “When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect.”

articles.title_orig: Public Radio Audience Continues "Impressive" Financial Support
articles.title_zh: Public Radio Audience Continues "Impressive" Financial Support
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Headlines
Public radio continues to face steep budget deficits after the loss of federal funding. But the surge in donor support in 2025 has largely carried over into 2026, according to the latest Public Radio Techsurvey from Jacobs Media.
Many in the pubcasting community have wondered if donations might slow down over time.
In conjunction with the Public Media Content Collective, Public Radio Techsurvey 2026 gathered input from 17,000 core public radio listeners using email databases of 49 U.S. stations. Jacobs cautioned that the survey does not represent all public radio listeners and is not stratified to the U.S. population.
Fred Jacobs, president of Jacobs Media, said in an online presentation that stations can stave off the effects of government cuts by using smart fundraising measures.
“Up to 72% strongly agree or agree that as a result of the political climate out there, they’re actually increasing their support to public radio, whether we’re talking generations, gender or format. This is truly a great sign, and I think maybe one of the most important slides in the entire deck,” Jacobs said.
Of the core listeners participating in the survey, four of every 10 say they donate every year, but this year they increased their donations, he said. See below (you can click on these slides to enlarge).
Political conditions continue to have a major impact on core public radio listeners, which is fueling fundraising, he said.
In fact, 39% strongly agree that what’s happening in politics will lead them to increase their support for public radio. The research found that women are more likely to feel that way than men.
“There’s a strong possibility that next year will be pretty solid as well,” Jacobs said.
One in five station listeners in the survey anticipate donating a greater amount next year than usual.
The most effective funding pitch for public radio stations (72%) is government funding cuts and the need for listener support. That’s followed by appeals of making public media available for all and then the need to support independent media in the community.
Current economic pressures were also measured. The Techsurvey shows that the economy is affecting the ability of respondents to give. More than half say it is having a negative impact on their spending.
“One in 10 core public radio listeners say they are being affected in a major way, a negative impact in their life as a result of the economy, and then 43% are saying the economy is having a significant effect, negative impact,” Jacobs said.
The public radio “net promoter” score remained at 70 for the second year in a row. It’s ahead of commercial radio but below Christian music radio results, Jacobs said.
Net promoter scores gauge whether core listeners are likely to recommend a public radio station to others. Public radio’s score has remained fairly steady since 2009, spiking to 75 during the covid pandemic.
“I think you’re definitely looking at reactions to the federal cuts as part of this year. In contrast, commercial radio has an average net promoter score of only 48, so that’s quite a gap there. Christian music radio, on the other hand, actually has a whopping 82,” Jacobs said.
When examining the three prominent formats of public radio –—AAA, classical and news/talk — clearly AAA is the big leader with a net promoter score of 80.
“By the way, that’s no fluke. It has been trending that way over the past several years. News/talk fans are the toughest graders with a score of only a 66,” he said.
Those who like public radio spend the vast majority of their time listening. In fact 40% say it’s all they listen to, Jacobs said. An equal amount say they listen to public radio most of the time. Women are the most likely to say they listen all the time, with millennials and Gen X listening less than boomers and the “greatest generation.”
However the aging of the largest subset of public radio core listeners is a concern. “Demos remain in Medicare territory,” Jacobs said.
The average age of those participating in this research project is 66.5 years old, compared to 65 three years ago. Sixty-five percent of listeners in the survey are 65 or up, according to Jacobs.
“The aging of public radio has been a long-time concern. Stations need to look for content, events and connections to achieve greater relevance with younger fans. Generational common threading is important strategically,” Jacobs said.
The study found that being local can give public stations an edge in their market. Nearly 75% agree that it does. It is the case especially among progressively younger Techsurvey respondents, Jacobs says. Men and women are about even in the findings.
However, only 39% strongly agree that the local public radio station they listen to is “well-connected in the local community.” Meanwhile, 46% want their station to have greater visibility in the community.
In the next part of our series about the Public Radio Techsurvey 2026, we will examine how in-car listening dropped even further as listening habits continue to shift to digital.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks says it’s focused on turnaround after report it explored Chipotle merger
articles.title_zh: Starbucks says it’s focused on turnaround after report it explored Chipotle merger
articles.content_orig:
Wall Street was buzzing Thursday about a possible merger that would amount to much more than a hill of beans.
Starbucks said it was focused on its turnaround plan after the Financial Times reported that it explored a potential deal to take over Chipotle Mexican Grill.
“Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy,” Starbucks said in a statement. “We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential.”
It added that it typically doesn’t comment on what it described as “rumors and speculation” and said it looks forward to sharing its next earnings results later in October.
The FT reported that Starbucks had hired advisers in recent months to work on a takeover proposal for Chipotle. NBC News hasn’t confirmed the report.
A tie-up between the two companies would mean a massive shake-up in the restaurant industry, which is grappling with consumers’ changing their spending and eating habits.
Before the report emerged, sending shares of Chipotle higher by 6.2%, the company had a total market value of about $39 billion. For comparison, Starbucks’ market value is at more than $105 billion.
Chipotle didn’t reply to a request for comment Thursday afternoon.
A deal would also reunite Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol with the company he led before he jumped to Starbucks in 2024.
Investors appeared worried that a deal could be a distraction for Niccol and his company. Starbucks shares fell as much as 6.6% on Thursday but closed the day only slightly lower.
The company is in the midst of a wide-ranging turnaround plan engineered by Niccol, including a redesign of Starbucks stores, new service standards to speed up customers’ orders, a refreshed menu and a reboot for its rewards program.
Just weeks ago, Niccol touted the plan’s results , saying “tremendous progress” has been made. Shareholders have seen promising returns, too. For the year, Starbucks shares are up almost 11%.
That closely tracks with the S&P 500’s 13% return so far this year. Starbucks has also far outperformed the negative 6.7% return that the S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary sector has recorded this year.
Chipotle shares have sagged by more than 11% this year and more than 20% over the last 12 months.
In July, the company’s latest earnings results beat expectations, but that followed a period of slow traffic and price hikes. Those results also came alongside soaring gas prices for consumers.
“We’re seeing encouraging progress because we’re focused on the right growth drivers,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said in a statement in July . Like Starbucks, Chipotle has also revamped its rewards program and made tweaks to its menu to lure customers back.
Chipotle has also started expanding outside the U.S., with plans to open stores in Mexico, South Korea and Saudi Arabia.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration freezes green cards for Microsoft, IT firms, probes universities
articles.title_zh: Trump administration freezes green cards for Microsoft, IT firms, probes universities
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft and Adobe from its Permanent Labor Certification program on Thursday, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said, as the Trump administration continues to take aim at immigration and foreign hiring programs ahead of November's midterm elections.
Sonderling said the Labor Department won't accept or process any new applications under the program for a host of companies, including Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro and HCL.
The secretary said Adobe and Microsoft were also suspended "due to multiple active federal investigations."
"Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers," Sonderling said.
Vice President JD Vance criticized Microsoft specifically, pointing to the firm's 6,000 layoffs in 2025. Vance claimed that the company "replaced" those workers with people on H-1B visas.
"So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first," Vance said.
Microsoft responded to Vance's claims and defended its hiring practices in a statement Thursday, saying "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans."
"Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees," the company said.
President Donald Trump is set to award the National Medal of Science to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other leading technology CEOs on Thursday at the same summit where the suspension announcement was made.
Nadella is from India and moved to the U.S. in 1988. He joined Microsoft in 1992.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su are also being honored at Thursday's medal ceremony. Each of the leaders immigrated to the U.S. Musk was born in South Africa and Su and Huang were born in Taiwan.
"It's one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk," Vance said. "I think 99% of American citizens look at somebody like Elon Musk or Lisa Su, the CEO of AMD, and they say, obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that."
Tech giants like Microsoft, Google , Amazon and Apple have been among the top sponsors of H-1B visas for decades. This year, Amazon had the highest number of petitions at 35,426 workers, followed by Cognizant and EY, according to 2026 data from Levels.fyi .
Microsoft was a close fourth at 21,706 petitions for 2026, with a median base salary of $180,710.
Microsoft said that petitions were only filed for workers "who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and said Microsoft's wages for H-1B workers were among the highest of all H-1B filings.
CNBC has reached out to Adobe for comment.

articles.title_orig: Spargursville airman accounted for from World War II
articles.title_zh: Spargursville airman accounted for from World War II
articles.content_orig:
The Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency announced Wednesday that U.S. Army Air Forces Staff Sgt. Given C. Grooms, 21, of Spargursville, Ohio, who was killed during World War II, was accounted for on June 9, 2026.
Grooms’s family recently received their full briefing on his identification; therefore, additional details on his identification can be shared.
In the winter of 1944, Grooms was assigned to the 718th Bombardment Squadron, 449th Bombardment Group, in Italy. On Jan. 30, he was serving as the radio operator aboard a B-24 Liberator bomber on a mission to Udine, Italy. The plane was shot down while returning from its mission and was last sighted north of the Isle of Morgo off the Italian coast near the town of Grado.
Three crew members made it out of the plane before the crash, but only one survived. The other seven members, including Grooms, were believed to have still been in the aircraft when it crashed.
Beginning in 1946, the American Graves Registration Service, U.S. Army Quartermaster Corps, was the organization tasked with recovering missing American service members in the Mediterranean Theater of Operations. AGRS investigators believed the aircraft crashed into the Adriatic Sea, so did not explore the marshy areas near Grado for wreckage. No remains recovered in the vicinity of Grado were ever associated with Grooms, and he was declared non-recoverable in August 1949.
In February 2010, a team of historians from a DPAA-predecessor organization traveled to the Isle of Morgo to investigate a lead on a possible WWII aircraft crash. Testimony from a local witness and 1945 aerial imagery of the site led the investigators to a duck pond and fish farm, where the team conducted a metal detector survey, finding a series of signals in the pond and along the southern bank.
In 2014, a team collecting additional pre-excavation data discovered human remains that were later identified as a crew member from Grooms’s aircraft. DPAA partnered with East Carolina University in early 2018 to conduct an additional survey for more accurate information in preparation for an excavation.
Four recovery efforts, led by DPAA partners Southeastern Archaeological Research, Tamarix Società Agricola Srls, and Isola Di Morgo Srl, were conducted between 2022 and 2025, finding aircraft wreckage, material evidence, life support equipment, and human remains, which was subsequently accessioned into the DPAA laboratory for scientific analysis.
To identify Grooms’ remains, scientists from DPAA used anthropological and dental analysis, as well as material evidence. Additionally, scientists from the Armed Forces Medical Examiner System used mitochondrial DNA, Y chromosome DNA, and autosomal DNA analysis.
Grooms’ name is recorded on the Tablets of the Missing at Florence American, an American Battle Monuments Commission site in Impruneta, Italy, along with the others missing from WWII. A rosette will be placed next to his name to indicate he has been accounted for.
Grooms will be buried in Waverly, Ohio, on Oct. 10.

articles.title_orig: Chinese military facility in Laos raises questions about Beijing’s Indo-Pacific reach - VOA
articles.title_zh: Chinese military facility in Laos raises questions about Beijing’s Indo-Pacific reach - VOA
articles.content_orig:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article .
New satellite imagery shows Chinese-made light attack aircraft and military vehicles deployed at a newly opened Chinese-supported air facility in Laos, fueling debate among security analysts over whether the site could eventually expand Beijing’s military reach and intelligence-gathering capabilities in mainland Southeast Asia. The Ban Keun Airport, about 50 kilometers northwest of the Lao capital Vientiane, was officially inaugurated by China and Laos as the “China-Laos Ban Keun Airport Joint Support and Training Center” and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy. Satellite imagery taken September 30 showed eight aircraft and more than 20 military vehicles at the site, according to a Reuters report. Analysts identified the aircraft as Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet trainers, also known as K-8 light attack aircraft. The facility currently has a roughly 2,000-meter paved runway, alongside aircraft parking areas, a control tower and newly constructed buildings. China’s Defense Ministry says the center is intended to help Laos strengthen the training of air force pilots and is “not directed against any third party.”
Some analysts say its longer-term significance, however, could go beyond pilot training.
Su Tzu-yun, director of the Division of Defense Strategy and Resources at Taiwan’s Institute for National Defense and Security Research, told VOA that if the runway is eventually extended to about 3,000 meters, it could accommodate larger Chinese bombers, transport aircraft and aerial refueling planes. Deployment of longer-range combat aircraft theoretically could extend Chinese air power toward the Strait of Malacca and, with aerial refueling, farther into the Indian Ocean, he said.
Su said the location has limitations because landlocked Laos is surrounded by countries whose airspace could constrain Chinese operations. He sees Ban Keun as part of a broader effort by Beijing, though, to develop strategic access across mainland Southeast Asia. “This is one of the main reasons China promoted the Belt and Road Initiative after Xi Jinping took office,” Su told VOA. “Through economic incentives, it invests in ports and airports in other developing countries, but behind that are strategic and military purposes.” China has invested heavily in regional infrastructure, including the China-Laos railway, while expanding its military presence elsewhere, most notably at its base in Djibouti and through its involvement at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base. Su said the combination of transportation infrastructure, ports and potential military access could give China alternative routes connecting the Pacific and Indian oceans and reduce its vulnerability if maritime supply lines through the Strait of Malacca were disrupted. But other analysts caution against overstating Ban Keun’s immediate military importance. Collin Koh, a maritime security specialist at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, told VOA by email that Ban Keun currently has “more political-symbolic significance than actual operational significance.” Nonetheless, he said the facility could support China’s growing defense diplomacy in Southeast Asia, including serving as a logistical stop during joint military exercises. It also may have value for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, Koh said. “Ban Keun could also serve as a base for intelligence and surveillance missions, mainly monitoring Thailand’s Isaan region,” he said. “Various multinational military exercises are routinely held in this area, such as Cope Tiger involving Thailand, the United States and Singapore.” Koh said China’s relationship with neighboring Myanmar does not necessarily mean Beijing will gain military access there. Myanmar is seeking to rebuild relations with other regional countries, he said, including India, which is particularly sensitive to potential Chinese military expansion toward the Indian Ocean. Additionally, the emerging Chinese presence in Laos is drawing attention because of its proximity to Vietnam. Alexander Vuving, a Vietnam specialist at the Daniel K. Inouye Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies in Hawaii, was cited by Taiwan’s Central News Agency as saying Chinese access at Ban Keun, combined with its presence at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base, could increase strategic pressure on Vietnam from its west and southwest. Chinese military commentator Song Zhongping rejected suggestions that Beijing is establishing a network of bases aimed at neighboring countries. He told VOA that China’s activities at Ban Keun and Ream should not be characterized as traditional military bases and stated that the limited deployments are designed to protect Chinese interests and support missions, such as counterterrorism, anti-piracy, and humanitarian assistance. “China now has three aircraft carrier battle groups, and we already possess a basic capability to project military power overseas,” Song said. “We do not necessarily need to establish so-called military bases in other countries.” For now, analysts interviewed by VOA generally agree the facility is unlikely to significantly alter the regional military balance, though its development is being closely watched as China expands its economic, diplomatic and security footprint across Southeast Asia.

articles.title_orig: Mortgage rates hit 7.4 percent for first time since November 2023
articles.title_zh: Mortgage rates hit 7.4 percent for first time since November 2023
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."

articles.title_orig: How a U.S. Diplomat Suppressed and Altered Reports Critical of Israel
articles.title_zh: How a U.S. Diplomat Suppressed and Altered Reports Critical of Israel
articles.content_orig:
David Milstein, a senior advisor to US Ambassador Mike Huckabee to Israel, used his position to quash reports on Israeli activities in the West Bank "to present the Netanyahu government in a favorable light" to Washington, the New York Times reported on Thursday.
The report is based on 15 anonymous sources that either work or interact with Milstein in both Jerusalem and Washington, the NYT said.
The NYT report alleged that Milstein enabled an annexation effort of the West Bank by assisting in the acceleration of Israeli settlements in the region primarily by suppressing reporting that would upset the Trump administration.
For example, the NYT said that Milstein blocked reports suggesting the Israeli government was failing to take action against violent settler extremists, instead sending a cable "praising Israel for 'cracking down' on the attacks."
In another instance, the report claims that a detailed report, written by embassy staff in response to a request by members of Congress to look into the death of Palestinian-Americans, was suppressed.
The NYT was told by sources that Milstein insisted on approving communications from the embassy upon his 2025 arrival in Jerusalem. Sources claimed the number of cables sent per month between the two countries dropped significantly after he took office.
Reviewing and editing diplomatic cables is a standard administrative function of ambassadors and senior staffers.
Huckabee has responded to the NYT report, excoriating the publication for using "cowardly 'anonymous sources,'" while accusing it of refusing to use a statement he gave when asked for comment.
The Times report , however, said that Huckabee declined interview requests.
In a post on X/Twitter, Huckabee slammed the report.
"The elements of the story the New York Times is trying to assemble are so lacking in fact that it ranks up with other Times farcical endeavors like the embarrassing 'dog rape' story, or the totally debunked story about a small boy being shot in the face by IDF in Gaza ," Huckabee wrote.
He continued his X post, writing that he "personally and categorically refute the elements of your proposed ‘story’ and I’m surprised that you expect to be taken seriously with such nonsense without even one named source."
The ambassador then threatened that the NYT could face litigation for defamation.
"You should consult your attorneys as to whether publishing such drivel could subject the Times to litigation for defamation. There is a reason [US President Donald Trump] calls them 'Fake News,'" he wrote.
Former US ambassador to Israel David Friedman also took to X to defend Milstein, calling the NYT report a "hit piece" based solely on anonymous sources, before offering his own testimony.
"Well, here’s a non-anonymous source who would have refuted this nonsense: me!" he wrote.
"David worked for me for several years when I was the US Ambassador to Israel. The Times knows me well and knows how to reach me. But they never did. Had the Times reached out, I would have categorically refuted its baseless claims."
Milstein served as an aide to US Senator Ted Cruz from 2013 to 2018 before becoming an assistant to Friedman until 2021. He returned to the role in 2025 under Huckabee during the second Trump administration .

articles.title_orig: Alabama modifies game-day plans ahead of Georgia game due to expected weather conditions
articles.title_zh: Alabama modifies game-day plans ahead of Georgia game due to expected weather conditions
articles.content_orig:
The University of Alabama is modifying several game-day operations ahead of Saturday’s football game against Georgia as severe weather and strong winds are expected to affect parts of Central Alabama.
The game remains scheduled to be played as planned at this time, but university officials are urging fans to closely monitor weather conditions and make informed decisions about travel and shelter.
The changes come as Tropical Storm Watches are in effect across much of Central Alabama amid strengthening conditions in the Gulf of Mexico. Forecasters are warning of potentially damaging winds, heavy rainfall, flash flooding and possible tornadoes over the weekend.
The National Weather Service in Birmingham has issued watches for numerous counties, including Jefferson, Shelby, Tuscaloosa, Bibb, Chilton and Talladega. Wind gusts could reach 55 mph in the Birmingham metro area, while some southern portions of the state could see gusts between 65 and 75 mph.
Those winds could down trees and power lines, block roads and cause power outages.
To reduce the risk to fans and prevent damage from the expected weather, tailgating will not be permitted on the University of Alabama campus before noon Saturday.
After noon, personal tailgating will be allowed only in uncovered areas, weather permitting.
The university said no tailgate drop-offs or setups will be allowed anywhere on campus Friday. Any tailgating supplies placed on campus before noon Saturday will be removed and discarded.
Corporate tailgating vendors, including Gameday Done Right, will not set up on the Quad because of the forecast for severe weather and high winds overnight Friday.
Fans may access the Quad and other campus gathering areas after noon, but those areas will first need to be inspected and determined to be safe. The university said there will be no Saturday tailgate supply drop-off for the Quad.
Electrical and power services will not be restored to the Quad until university officials determine conditions are safe.
The university also said it could further delay operations if weather conditions warrant.
Campus parking lots and shuttle services are currently scheduled to open at noon Saturday.
Fans attempting to park on campus before the lots officially open will be turned away. Parking pass holders who purchased parking through Clutch! will receive direct updates if conditions change.
Shuttle buses will begin operating once parking lots open, unless sustained winds cause additional delays.
Visitors using off-campus parking are encouraged to check with individual parking operators for potential schedule changes.
Several activities scheduled ahead of the game have also been canceled or modified because of the expected weather.
All activities on and around the Quad have been canceled, as have all Champions Lane activities.
The planned 8 p.m. Friday announcement at Gorgas Library celebrating the successful conclusion of the Rising Tide 2.0 capital campaign has also been canceled.
The Elephant Stomp is not currently planned.
The Walk of Champions is expected to continue approximately 2 hours before kickoff, weather permitting.
ESPN's College GameDay will be held inside Coleman Coliseum.
The north and east doors are scheduled to open at 5:30 a.m., with fans allowed to begin lining up at 5:15 a.m.
Because of the expected weather, overnight queuing and camping outside Coleman Coliseum will not be permitted.
Fans attending College GameDay should also be aware that only clear bags will be allowed inside the venue and will be inspected upon entry. The field-goal kick associated with the program will take place inside Coleman Coliseum.
University officials said weather conditions and game-day operations could continue to change as the storm system develops.
Fans are encouraged to monitor official University of Alabama News, UA Gameday and UA Safety communications, including social media and university apps, for updates concerning weather, parking, tailgating and other game-day operations.
The university said the changes are intended to help provide a safe game-day environment while weather conditions remain uncertain.

articles.title_orig: Grandmother of 12 holds plank for 5 hours in new world record attempt - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Grandmother of 12 holds plank for 5 hours in new world record attempt - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
A grandmother of 12 is being credited for breaking her own Guinness World Record for a woman holding a plank move for the longest time period.
DonnaJean Wilde made her potential record-breaking attempt at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week and completed a plank hold for five hours.
Guinness World Records confirmed to ABC News that Wilde's title record, which she achieved on March 21, 2024, is 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds. The organization said it has received an application for Wilde's newest record attempt and will review evidence before declaring a new record.
"I always wondered if I could have gone to five [hours]," Wilde told ABC News' Danny New of her motivation to break her own plank hold record.
According to World Senior Games, the record attempt began at 3:03 p.m. MT, with judges rotating out every hour until 8:03 p.m. MT, when WIlde's attempt ended.
"Some of them would come right down to me: 'Go, DonnaJean, go! You're doing great!'" Wilde said of the judges.
The 61-year-old -- who lives in Alberta, Canada -- said her training to prepare for her record attempt included having her 3-year-old granddaughter, Rose, lie on her back while she planked.
Wilde said she wasn't certain she would be able to accomplish her five-hour feat and even considered giving up during the attempt.
"I told [my husband] Randy, 'I'm done. I'm going down.' And they [the audience] all chanted me to the end. They got me through the last 10 minutes," Wilde said.
If her latest record attempt is recognized, Wilde would have earned her third Guinness title, following her previous plank record and her other record for the most pushups done in an hour by a woman, at 1,575.
It's another impressive feat for Wilde, who said she didn't rest for long after her latest plank feat. The morning after her record attempt, she ran in a 3,000-meter race.
As for her next record attempt, Wilde said she hopes to do at least 1,600 pushups in an hour and break her second record title.

articles.title_orig: Florida health officials meet amid fierce debate over childhood vaccine plans
articles.title_zh: Florida health officials meet amid fierce debate over childhood vaccine plans
articles.content_orig:
Heather Hazzan / Self magazine
Last month, a child in Montana died of Haemophilus influenzae type b, better known as Hib. According to the state health department, the child had not received the Hib vaccine , and Montana's four other pediatric deaths from H influenzae since 2012 were all caused by strains the vaccine doesn't cover. That makes this the state's first pediatric Hib death in at least 14 years.
Many parents have never heard of Hib, because the vaccine worked so well that the disease all but disappeared. Public health is often called a victim of its own success, and Florida's proposal could make children the victims instead.
Tomorrow, Florida's Department of Health will hold a public hearing on its plan to remove requirements for four vaccines that protect against Hib, pneumococcal disease, hepatitis B, and chickenpox. The Hib and pneumococcal vaccines are currently required for daycare and preschool, while hepatitis B and chickenpox are required through K-12.
State officials have framed the change as a matter of parental rights and "medical freedom," and the department hasn't pointed to any new evidence about the safety or effectiveness of these vaccines. The department can remove these four through its rulemaking authority, while measles and polio requirements are written into state law and would need action from the legislature.
These four vaccines also protect against the diseases parents are least likely to remember, which makes them the easiest to give up. Florida is the first state to propose this, and health departments in some other states have similar authority to try it.
Before Hib vaccines came into wide use in the late 1980s, Hib was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in American children under 5 years, and about one in 200 kids developed invasive Hib disease by age 5. Each year, roughly 20,000 young children got severe Hib disease, and about 1,000 died. Among children who survived Hib meningitis, 15% to 30% were left with hearing loss or other permanent neurologic damage.
Pediatricians who trained in that era still talk about it (and the clinicians we work with often name Hib as one of the scariest vaccine-preventable diseases). MaryAnne, who shared her story with Voices for Vaccines , nearly died of Hib at age 4 in the early 1960s, when an infection of her epiglottis left her unable to breathe and doctors performed an emergency tracheotomy.
These four vaccines also protect against the diseases parents are least likely to remember, which makes them the easiest to give up.
Once the vaccine became routine, cases in young children dropped by 99% , and in 2022 the United States recorded just 17 confirmed cases in children under 5. Provisional surveillance data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show 28 cases so far this year.
Florida pediatricians have been warning about an increase in Hib cases for months. At a state workshop on the proposal last December, a Panama City pediatrician said he had seen two unvaccinated children with Hib in the intensive care unit in the previous six months, a 4-month-old who died and a 2½-year-old left “brain dead.”
All four diseases are easy to underestimate, and for Hib, the name is part of the reason. The bacterium was first identified during an influenza outbreak in 1892, before scientists knew a virus caused the flu. The “influenzae” part of its name makes it sound like something a flu shot would cover.
Pneumococcal disease is just as unfamiliar to most parents, even though, before the vaccine, about one in 500 US 1-year-olds developed a serious invasive infection like meningitis or a bloodstream infection each year. Many adults remember chickenpox as a harmless rite of passage, even though before the vaccine it caused 10,500 to 13,500 hospitalizations and 100 to 150 deaths in this country each year. Hepatitis B tends to be thought of as an adult disease, even though about 90% of babies who become infected develop chronic infection, and about a quarter of people chronically infected during childhood eventually die early from cirrhosis or liver cancer.
When a vaccine works, the disease disappears from daily life, along with the stories and firsthand experience that once made the vaccine feel necessary. For most families, the last time anyone saw these diseases up close was a generation or more ago. Measles still has some cultural memory (and plenty of recent headlines), while most parents today have never known a child with Hib meningitis.
That gap makes it easy to frame these four shots as optional extras, and it helps explain why Florida's proposal has drawn far less public outrage than a move against the measles vaccine would.
When a vaccine works, the disease disappears from daily life, along with the stories and firsthand experience that once made the vaccine feel necessary.
Supporters point out that removing a requirement doesn't take the vaccine away, and parents can still choose it. In practice, decades of research link stronger school requirements with higher vaccination rates, and easier exemptions with higher exemption rates and more disease.
Florida is starting from a weak position, too, with kindergarten vaccination coverage falling substantially in recent years, from at least 93.5% for major required vaccines in 2019-20 to 88.9% of kindergarteners fully vaccinated in 2025-26. Requirements also prompt the pediatrician visit and records check that catch a missed dose before a child starts daycare or school.
Even with the governor's support, no Florida legislator filed a bill to repeal the state's school vaccine laws in any of its 2026 sessions, and no state has repealed its school vaccination laws outright.
But the health department route doesn't need legislators at all, and many states give their health departments authority over which vaccines are required for school (how much varies by state), which means appointed officials in those states could do what Florida's surgeon general is attempting.
Anti-vaccine advocates are already pushing Louisiana, Texas, and Idaho to follow Florida's lead. In each state, the most exposed vaccines will be the ones that aren't written into statute and that parents are least likely to defend. If Florida's rule is approved, other states with similar rules could follow the same process.
Public support for school requirements remains strong, and 81% of US parents back requiring measles and polio vaccines for school, with some exceptions, although those aren't the vaccines on the table in Florida. That support goes only so far if parents don't know what Hib, pneumococcus, hepatitis B, and chickenpox did to children before we had vaccines.
For those of us in public health and medicine, the job is to make these diseases familiar again with facts and real cases. Clinicians can share what they've seen, health departments can report cases and deaths quickly and clearly, and communicators can talk about these four vaccines with the same urgency we bring to measles.
States also need to know where coverage is slipping. Montana is the only state that doesn't require school districts to report vaccination data to its health department, and legislators voted down a bill to change that last year, just as measles returned to the state for the first time in 35 years.
Hib became a disease most parents have never heard of because vaccination made it rare. But keeping it rare means maintaining the high vaccination rates that requirements help sustain.
Dr. Steier is a public health scientist and scientific communicator. She is the founder of Unbiased Science , an organization that uses data visualizations, real-world analogies, and human voice to communicate complex scientific concepts for public understanding via multiple media modalities.

articles.title_orig: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
articles.title_zh: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
articles.content_orig:
After having faced fierce backlash, President Donald Trump on Wednesday sought to clean up incendiary comments he made earlier this week, when he said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego.
Trump’s original remarks , made at a campaign rally in Nebraska, seemed to refer to what would happen if Iran had a nuclear weapon.
“They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said Monday to cheers from the crowd.
He recast those remarks Wednesday night at a rally in San Antonio as he tried to explain the Iran war, saying he had “no choice” if the U.S. were to keep Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
“You want to see problems? And I said it the other day: Let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit. You want to see a horror show? You want to see problems?”
“Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles if you want to see some bad things happen. You want to see a country that would be in free fall?”
This time, however, he added: “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country. We’re not letting that happen.”
Trump’s initial remarks sparked backlash, particularly from California Democrats. Gov. Gavin Newsom accused Trump of prodding foreign enemies to take out U.S. cities. “He is deranged and dangerous,” Newsom wrote on social media.
“To do that makes us look ridiculous on the world stage, but it also gives a green light to Iran, the nation that he chose to attack, the green light to attack our cities,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass told NBC News after Wednesday’s rally.
Bass said she may call on Congress to investigate Trump’s comments.
Trump’s comments Wednesday came in a winding speech at a boisterous rally that stretched for about an hour and 45 minutes, with numerous interruptions from protesters. At one point, a protester who had been heckling Trump was grabbed by a person in the audience in an incident captured on video. A man in the crowd, wearing what looked to be a red “Make America Great Again” hat, grabbed the protester by the hair. Others in the crowd tried to free the protester.
The evening was meant to boost Texas Republicans, including Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for the Senate in a pitched battle against Democrat James Talarico. In a reflection of Trump’s low favorability ratings, even in the red state of Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott — a staunch Trump ally — said he could not attend because of a scheduling conflict.
Capping the night, Trump announced that he would award former Major League Baseball pitcher and seven-time Cy Young Award winner Rogers Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
“We’re giving him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and along with the Congressional Medal of Honor, it’s the highest award bestowed upon anyone,” Trump said, adding he would help him get into the Baseball Hall of Fame someday. “He deserves it.”
Clemens, a Texan, was accused of using performance-enhancing drugs late in his baseball career. He maintains he has never used PEDs.
On Wednesday night, Clemens took the stage at Trump’s invitation, saying he was “stunned.”
“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” Clemens said. “To get it from this man, this president, there wouldn’t be another president I’d want to get it from.”
Natasha Korecki is a senior national political reporter for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.
Bill Feather is an assignment editor for NBC Los Angeles who covers general assignment and daily breaking news, primarily in Southern California.

Global Finance named the World's Safest Banks 2026 on October 6, 2026 — marking the 35th consecutive year the publication has ranked the world's most financially secure banks.
The World’s Safest Banks ranking is a trusted benchmark used by corporate treasurers, institutional investors, and financial institutions to evaluate counterparty strength and long-term stability. “In a period of continued economic uncertainty, geopolitical tension and rapid change across the financial sector, strength, stability and disciplined risk management remain critical measures of banking excellence,” said Joseph Giarraputo, founder and editorial director of Global Finance. “Global Finance’s World’s Safest Banks 2026 recognizes the institutions that have demonstrated the financial strength and long-term resilience needed to navigate emerging risks and provide confidence to customers and markets
Global Finance ranks the World’s Safest Banks using long-term foreign currency credit ratings assigned by the three major international rating agencies — Moody’s , Standard & Poor’s (S&P) , and Fitch Ratings. Key criteria include:
Rating sources: Only long-term foreign currency ratings from Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch are used. National scale ratings are excluded.
Eligibility: Banks must rank among the 500 largest in the world by total assets that hold at least two credit agency ratings.
Objectivity: Drawing from all three agencies ensures results are consistent and comparable across countries and regions.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX takes aim at US wireless carriers with spectrum acquisition
articles.title_zh: SpaceX takes aim at US wireless carriers with spectrum acquisition
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX announced an agreement on Thursday to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio as it pushes its Starlink service deeper into the U.S. telecommunications market. Shares of AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile tumbled in extended trading.
The deal involves the acquisition of a spectrum portfolio from Grain Management, which specializes in digital infrastructure, and is subject to approval by the Federal Communications Commission. SpaceX said in a statement that it's a "license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band."
"This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," SpaceX said.
In a post on X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk called it a "very big deal."
Last week, T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon formed a joint venture "focused on expanding coverage in underserved areas," via satellite and direct-to-device (D2D) services, and Starlink was notably absent. T-Mobile has also previously removed mention of Starlink from its T-Satellite promotions.
SpaceX appears determined to battle telecommunications giants in the U.S., and deliver its own services without them.
"This adds fuel to the fire in the battle between SpaceX and the mobile operators," said TMF Associates' Tim Farrar, an industry expert. "But it's still a very limited amount of spectrum and to get reliable building penetration in urban areas SpaceX would have to deploy towers on the ground."
The announcement comes a day after the FCC said it would vote on a proposal to auction 25 megahertz of "prime spectrum" to support D2D services from satellites to smart phones. The FCC also said it would vote Oct. 29 on taking public comment on a proposal to make an additional 482MHz of spectrum available for supplemental coverage from space and to modernize FCC rules for D2D services in the licensed spectrum.
The two proposals could benefit SpaceX as well as Amazon , which has also moved to build a service with satellite networks.
SpaceX, which went public in June in a record IPO and is now valued at over $2 trillion, has relied on Starlink as its cash cow and only profitable business segment to date.
The service is available in 205 countries and had 12 million subscribers as of June 30, according to SpaceX's second-quarter report. The connectivity business generated $1.66 billion in operating income in the period on $4.29 billion in revenue. Starlink is the largest global satellite communications network with over 11,000 satellites in orbit.
Deutsche Bank analysts, who recommend buying SpaceX stock, estimated in a report this week that Starlink's global subscriber base reached 13.5 million at the end of September, including 4.1 million based in the U.S.
In its rocket business, SpaceX has reduced its planned cadence of launches for next year. The company is now looking to make its massive Starship rockets reliable and fully reusable in order to transition away from use of its smaller Falcon rockets. SpaceX is also building a cloud computing business and aims to someday build orbital data centers. For now, its space and artificial intelligence units are losing money.
SpaceX didn't immediately respond to a request for further information, including when its new services may come online if approved by regulators. If cleared, the added spectrum will help SpaceX combine satellite and ground-based coverage once it builds out a network of towers.
SpaceX shares rose about 2.5% in extended trading after dropping 4% during regular market hours.
